speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENDED SERVICES TO EUROPEAN POINTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement regarding the further development of international scheduled air line services by Canadian carriers.
Recently Canadian Pacific Air Lines company applied to the government for authorization to operate a scheduled service from Montreal to Lisbon, Portugal, under the existing bilateral air agreement between Canada and Portugal, and for authorization to extend this service to Madrid if and when appropriate arrangements with the Spanish government can be made. The new service would be operated in conjunction with the present C.P.A. service from Mexico and South America to Toronto but would not carry local traffic between Toronto and Montreal.
As has been indicated in previous statements of government policy, Trans-Canada Air Lines is the Canadian air carrier designated by the government to operate transAtlantic air services to European points. Trans-Canada Air Lines also has had before the government proposals for the extension of its trans-Atlantic services to additional points in Europe.
The government, after considering these matters, has taken the following action: (1) C.P.A. has been designated by the governor in council as the Canadian carrier to operate international scheduled air services from Montreal to Lisbon and also to Madrid if and when the necessary arrangements can be made with the Spanish government; and <2) the government has reaffirmed its policy that T.C.A. is and is to be the Canadian air carrier for service to other European points not at present served by a Canadian air carrier. T.C.A. at present provides service to London, Paris and Dusseldorf, and existing bilateral air agreements authorize a Canadian service to Brussels, Copenhagen, Oslo and Stockholm. It is expected that negotiations with the government of Switzerland will be initiated shortly looking to the conclusion of a bilateral agreement with that country.
I am not in a position to state when the carriers concerned will initiate the new services, and any announcement on these matters will be made by the air lines themselves.
During the discussions concerning the proposed service to Lisbon, C.P.A. indicated to the government that upon being licenced to operate over this new route it would apply to the air transport board for permission to give up its present domestic licence for service between Winnipeg and Churchill. The selection of a carrier to operate the Winnipeg-Churchill service will, of course, be a matter for determination in the usual manner by the air transport board.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last the hon. member for Quebec West asked me to offer some comment upon the newspaper article which he quoted and I am now glad to do so. [Mr. Marler.l
I have read the statement made by Mr. George Nagy, general secretary of the Hungarian federation of Canada, which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of February 12, 1957. My comments upon ti are as follows: It may be that there are amongst the Hungarian refugees arriving in Canada some who are security risks. At the present time, only a limited screening is possible although a certain number of refugees are being checked where circumstances point to the need for that action.
Speed in processing the Hungarian refugees is all important and I am sure that to attempt to do more than we are now doing in the way of screening would only delay the forward movement and thus impede the over-all plan for facilitating the flow of these people to Canada.
Canadian residents who have reason to believe that there are any subversive elements among the Hungarian refugees will, we feel sure, make it their duty to come forward with this information. As and when they do, they may be certain that what they have to tell will be welcomed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and other authorities and that it will be carefully studied and if necessary acted upon.
On the whole we are satisfied that there is only a slight security risk and it is more than counter-balanced by the worth of the many good citizens we are getting. I think that most of these refugees will recognize communist agitation for what it really is and will not be misled by it; for I do not know of any group of people less likely to be influenced by communist propaganda than exiles who have been driven from their homes as the victims of communist oppression. Advice, hospitality and a helpful hand by loyal Canadians with whom the refugees are in contact will, I feel, more than neutralize any harmful propaganda to which they may be subjected. Canadian citizens of Hungarian descent can be particularly helpful in this respect and Mr. Nagy's statement shows they are alive to the situation.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED DISCUSSIONS ON SUSPENSION OF NUCLEAR TESTS IN PACIFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, February 13, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) asked me to take notice of a question which appears at page 1245 of Hansard of that date:
Has the Prime Minister's attention been called to the report of the exchange between the governments of Japan and the United Kingdom on the suspension of nuclear tests in the Pacific, and can the Prime Minister inform the house if he and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom at their forthcoming meeting in Bermuda will discuss the suspension of these tests, which are described by every reputable scientist as dangerous and useless?
I have made inquiries and we have not had the exchanges between the governments of Japan and the United Kingdom formally drawn to our attention by either party. I doubt if we have any more information than the information which the hon. gentleman himself has and which has been public for some time. We have been aware for some months of the intention of the United Kingdom government to conduct a series of nuclear tests in the Pacific this year and I think that has been common knowledge since last spring. We have not contemplated suggesting to the United Kingdom authorities that this part of their program for the development of nuclear weapons should be suspended.
I would remind the house that we in Canada are to a large extent dependent upon the nuclear arsenals of the United Kingdom and the United States to provide a deterrent to aggression. It is in our interest that the deterrent be as effective as it can be and this is obviously the essential purpose of these tests.
I might add that we are very much alive to the possible hazards of radiation generated by nuclear explosions and this matter is under constant surveillance. Hon. members will recall that my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) recently made a statement in the house in this regard. It is our hope that measures can be agreed upon internationally to set bounds to whatever hazards may arise out of tests, and my colleagues, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard), during the course of the present session of the United Nations general assembly have emphasized
our hope that limitations on nuclear test explosions can be achieved. Together with Japan and Norway, Canada sponsored a proposal for the establishment, as a preliminary step, of a system for advance registration with the United Nations of nuclear test explosions. This proposal has been referred to the subcommittee of the disarmament commission of which Canada is a member and which is to meet in London beginning on March 18.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: As far as I know that report is entirely inaccurate and arises out of pure speculation by someone who is anxious to publish a story about it. The situation has not changed. The major part of those treasures are, I understand, in the custody of the curator of the Quebec museum in Quebec city. The Polish authorities have from time to time been informed that access to our courts is open to them to assert title to whatever treasures may be there. But the Polish authorities have not up to the present time chosen to have recourse to our courts. The government of Canada has no title under which it could resort to the courts to have the matter determined. I have not heard of any just recently, but there have been conversations from time to time between representatives of the Polish government in Canada and the Department of External Affairs. These representatives of the Polish government have been told constantly that this government has no authority to take disputed property and deliver it to the one it might think was the rightful owner.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED CAPITAL OF BOARD
speechtext:
In the amendment to the Canadian Farm Loan Act assented to last year the capital of the board was fixed at $3 million and authority was vested in the Minister of Finance to loan to the board from time to time up to twenty times the par value of the outstanding capital stock of the board. This would amount to $60 million. One of the purposes of last year's bill was that the board should, through the Minister of Finance, come to parliament periodically to increase its borrowing power. Previously the
82715-84J
Canadian Farm Loan Act capital of the board was increased automatically with an increase of its lending, in the ratio of 5 per cent of the total principal amount of loans outstanding, and it was mandatory for the Minister of Finance to subscribe to, and pay for, any increase in capital stock thus issued. The Minister of Finance was in turn authorized to lend to the board an amount not to exceed 20 times such outstanding capital stock of the board.
At the time of the last amendment to the Canadian Farm Loan Act it was anticipated that it would not be necessary to ask parliament for a further amendment until perhaps 1958 for the purpose of increasing the board's capital and thus increasing the Minister of Finance's lending authority to the board.
As of December 31, 1956, outstanding borrowings from the Minister of Finance totalled $43,300,000 leaving a balance of lending authorization to the Minister of Finance of $16,700,000. It is expected that the accelerated rate of lending will continue, and that the board's commitments for the period January 1, 1957 to March 31, 1958, will be as follows: loans now in solicitors' hands for disbursement, $4,100,000; loan approvals on hand pending acceptance by applicants, $4,700,000; unappraised applications on hand, $750,000; anticipated new business April 1, 1957 to March 31, 1958, $15,000,000. These items all total $24,550,000.
Now, on the other side there is a balance of lending authorization of the minister as of January 1, 1957, as I have previously described, of $16,700,000. It is estimated that the board will receive by principal repayments from January 1, 1957 to March 31, 1958, $6,000,000. These items would come to $22,700,000. In other words, there is a probable excess of commitments over present lending authority, if we look forward to March 31, 1958, of $1,850,000. Therefore, in the interests of the board's prospective borrowers, it seems desirable that the Canadian Farm Loan Act be amended at this time to increase the lending authority automatically of the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED CAPITAL OF BOARD
speechtext:
I should say at the outset that we in this group are pleased that this move is taking place to satisfy the need for credit among Canadian farmers. The very fact that the government has seen it necessary to increase the capitalization of the Canadian farm loan board from $3 million to $4 million shows the need for credit that exists in Canada today.
However, I should like to point out to the parliamentary assistant that this need for credit will not be exerted unless the general policy of the Canadian farm loan board is altered to allow farmers the ability to get more readily, this credit which they so direly need. The increase in the capitalization from $3 million to $4 million will be of little value unless the regulations which the Canadian farm loan board is following at the present time are relaxed.
The parliamentary assistant will recall that last year before the banking and commerce committee the Canadian federation of agriculture made certain recommendations and I should like to make this point. If some of these regulations are followed the increase in the capitalization will fall far short of the need in the very near future.
One of the points advocated by the Canadian federation of agriculture was an increase in the length of time for the repayment of the loan, and the insertion of more flexibility into the repayment to allow farmers to repay as their capabilities allow them. The contention there was the one that is generally advocated by farmers, that as they have good crops they are in a position to repay loans, and as they have crop failures they are not financially able to repay. The request was to have the organization of the farm loan board geared to this so that the farmers would not be required to make payments in years of crop failure. This, of course, would require an increase in the capitalization because it would need more working capital for the Canadian farm loan board.
Another factor which, if adopted, would certainly have an effect on this would be a change in the maximum percentage of the appraised value. Last year the act was amended to change it to 65 per cent of the

appraised value. But suppose the government should follow the recommendations of the Canadian federation of agriculture and other farm organizations and increase the appraised value to 80 per cent on the sum of $8,000, with a sliding scale for greater amounts which that organization has recommended, I think again we would find that the capitalization would fall far short of the need.
If we were to follow another recommendation which is made and reduce the interest rates to the cost of the money, plus the cost of the reserve, with the government bearing the interest charges, it would have the effect of increasing the availability of loans, or at least it would make an increased demand for the loans so that there would be a greater use for them. It was pointed out by Dr. Hope, the economist for the Canadian federation of agriculture, that although we have $4,500 million worth of agricultural land in Canada, only $40 million, or one-tenth of one per cent of the land value was covered by loans. This has increased this year, as the parliamentary assistant has pointed out, to $43 million. I would like to interject a point that a lot of this increased demand is resulting from the inflationary tendencies which are present in Canada today.
The chairman of the Canadian farm loan board, Mr. Chester, pointed out that 25 per cent of the loans of the Canadian farm loan board were made for the consolidation of debts, and he intimated that it had increased in significant amounts in the last two or three years. In the report of the Canadian farm loan board there is an indication that 30.1 per cent of the total lendings of the board have gone into consolidation of debt. Now we are getting into another very important aspect of the functions of the Canadian farm loan board. It is apparent that the primary purpose of the farm loan board is to allow the farmers to purchase more land so that they may be operating on an economic unit.
If agricultural circumstances in Canada demand that in order to survive the farmers are forced to borrow from the Canadian farm loan board for the consolidation of debt it is certainly limiting the amount they are able to get from the land. I noticed an article in the Globe and Mail on February 11 headed, "Consumer Debt Total has Bankers Worried". I do not think the bankers are nearly as worried as are those individuals who are in debt. The article points out that at the end of 1950 Canadians owed $1,034 million for the things they bought on time and in 1956 the total had leaped to $2,395 million.
I am injecting those figures into this debate because farmers are also in the category of
Canadian Farm Loan Act those who must incur consumer indebtedness. If consumer indebtedness has increased by this staggering amount in six years there is going to be a greatly increased demand for loans under the Canadian Farm Loan Act to consolidate the debt. This is one of the functions of the farm loan board and as I have pointed out more and more of the board's money is going toward the consolidation of debt all the time. If this tendency continues to increase we will eventually find that 40 or 50 per cent of the funds of the board are being used for the consolidation of debt.
I think the proportion that is used for the consolidation of debt has increased because of the reluctance of the board to loan money for agricultural purposes. Apparently this is done in carrying out the policy of the government but I think it is part and parcel of the problem of inflation. Inflation has always caused serious increases in the valuation of land and since the board makes loans on 65 per cent of the appraised value for production purposes of land it is going to be impossible for farmers to obtain loans as the actual land value increases. In some areas land values have doubled and nearly trebled in the last few years. It is not that the value of land has gone up, it is just that the value of the dollar has gone down. We therefore have the situation that the farmer is unable to borrow enough money in terms of the appraised value to pay for his lands.
I had an instance drawn to my attention where a farmer applied for a loan slightly in excess of $5,000 on the security of three-quarter sections of land but it was turned down because it was inadequate security on the basis of the productivity of that land and yet at the same time the land is selling for that amount of money per quarter section. It is part and parcel of this niggardly approach of the Canadian frrm loan board in failing to supply the real need for credit in Canada as far as land is concerned. The demand for credit for the purchase of farms and for the expansion of farms into economic units is going to increase very greatly during the next few years.
It has been pointed out in this house that the agricultural population in Canada is declining. The impact of this is quite readily visible and it will mean that available land will be established in larger areas. In turn this will mean that farmers will need funds to purchase land which is available in their proximity in order to have an economic holding for themselves. With the congested grain conditions and the low delivery quotas in western Canada it is extremely difficult for farmers to purchase land on terms with the finances they can obtain from any agency other than the Canadian farm loan board. If

Canadian Farm Loan Act the government were to follow the policy of liberalizing the loans and accept the recommendations of farm organizations by actively going out and obtaining as many loans as possible so that the cost of each loan would be reduced, I am convinced that the amount the parliamentary assistant has pointed out as the increase in capitalization from $3 million to $4 million would be quite inadequate to meet the need for credit for agricultural purposes and would fall far short of the demand. The policy should be geared to provide the maximum number of loans rather than the minimum. We have altogether too many instances where some technicality has prevented a farmer from obtaining a loan and some of these technicalities should be ironed out.
I recall another case where a farmer was unable to get a loan from the board because he did not in effect reside on the land. This, I might point out, does not make him a suitcase farmer. In many areas in western Canada the trend has developed where farmers reside in villages or towns where they have ready access to schools, hospitals, and other social services and travel 10 miles or so to farm their land. Under the present regulations they are denied a loan unless they actually reside on the farm or at least have some buildings on the farm. This is handicapping the granting of loans by the board and preventing it from developing into a credit agency.
My general comments with regard to this resolution would be to ask the assurance of the minister that this increase in capitalization will be sufficient, in view of the changes in the legislation which have been requested by the board, to make it a truly effective credit agency. It has been pointed out in previous debates how effective the Veterans' Land Act is in serving as a credit agency and assisting young farmers to establish themselves. The minister is well aware of this and he will have a realization of how changes could be made in the Canadian Farm Loan Act to render it effective in filling the role of providing credit to farmers so that they may become established with a good chance of being able to succeed even in the face of economic adversity. The government should go one step further and have the Canadian farm loan board follow the pattern of the farmers' home administration in the United States which, as the parliamentary assistant is aware, lends up to 100 per cent of the appraised value of the land and the loans are given the same degree of supervision as loans under the Veterans' Land Act. In other words under this policy the loan is made to establish the farmer. He has value as a human being and when his energy and

resources are applied to sufficient land he has a good chance of succeeding. As long as we are going to follow the policy of being as stingy as possible in making these loans, so stingy that only one-tenth of 1 per cent of all the land value in Canada has loans made against it, we are not going to be successful in achieving this objective.
I should like some clarification on these points and an indication from the parliamentary assistant as to whether, in view of these recommendations, the amount will in effect be sufficient to provide a true credit policy that will meet the crying need for credit among Canadian farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are very pleased to see this resolution brought before us again this year. We had a rather lengthy discussion last session regarding the Canadian farm loan board. About the only thing we gained from that lengthy discussion was an improvement in the application form that is used in applying for loans. I wish to commend the parliamentary assistant for this new type of application form which is simplified and more convenient for farmers to use.
Last year we advanced certain suggestions to the minister regarding the Canadian farm loan board. For example, we feel that there are several weaknesses in the regulations under which the act is administered. We felt last year and we still feel that the present maximum of 65 per cent of the appraised valuation of the land is too small. We asked last year and we are asking again that that 65 per cent maximum be increased to 80 per cent.
We feel that the appraisers of the Canadian farm loan board are definitely very conservative; they do not reflect one bit of liberal thought when they hand out their appraisals as far as the worth of the farmers' property is concerned. I have reason to know that this is true because I have had the opportunity to compare an appraisal given by a representative of the Veterans' Land Act on a certain piece of property with that given by a representative of the Canadian farm loan board and found that the appraisal given by the representative of the Veterans' Land Act was far more liberal than that in the case of the farm loan board.
We feel that the maximum amount of loan is far too low if we are to expect young people to buy farms. The maximum amount that can be borrowed from the Canadian farm loan board is $15,000, and these days $15,000 will not go very far in buying and equipping an efficient farm unit in western Canada. We are hoping that our young men will stay on

the farm and if they are to do that they must have some assistance. These days a farmer cannot afford to turn over his farm to his son for nothing because he needs the money on which to live. I suggest to the minister that he give serious consideration to increasing the maximum of the loan under the farm loan board from $15,000 to $20,000.
I submit that the farm loan board is charging a very high rate of interest as far as its loans are concerned. Surely this government should be able to provide the Canadian farm loan board with money to lend to farmers at less than 5 per cent.
We in this group feel that the term of the loan is too short and we would like to see it increased from 30 to 40 years. If that were done the annual instalments or payments would be cut down considerably.
In our part of Canada there is much concern with regard to the Canadian farm loan board. The farmers of Alberta particularly feel that this board is not offering the service it could offer. For example, the Alberta wheat pool has this to say about the farm loan board:
If the federal government wants to aid the farm economy, in ways that encourage real improvement in efficiency, it could become as generous in extending credit to the farmers as to the urban dwellers.
That is from the Wheat Pool Budget which contained an article from the Winnipeg Free Press which pointed out that the ordinary citizen of Canada can borrow from 70 per cent to 90 per cent of the cost of building a new home under the National Housing Act whereas a farmer can borrow only 65 per cent of the appraised value of the land up to $15,000 under the Canadian Farm Loan Act. In order to buy a $15,000 farm a farmer can borrow only $9,750, but a man building a $15,000 house can borrow $12,800. I suggest that that is just another example of this government not giving the farmers of Canada that to which they are rightly entitled, which is the same deal as is being given to other people in Canada. I trust that the minister and the government will soon start considering putting the farmer on an equal basis with the rest of the people living in Canada.
The Alberta Federation of Agriculture are much interested in improving the farm loan board. On January 31 of this year it appealed to the provincial government of Alberta for assistance in this regard, and I should like to quote now from an article in the Edmonton Journal of January 31. On that date a delegation representing the Alberta Federation of Agriculture met with the provincial cabinet in Edmonton, and according to the following report requested:
Action in support of a request to the federal government for long-term farm credit was urged
Canadian Farm Loan Act when a delegation from the Alberta Federation of Agriculture submitted resolutions passed at the recent provincial convention to the Alberta cabinet Tuesday.
And again:
The resolution on farm credit requested "the support and co-operation of the government of Alberta in urging the federal government to meet this credit need".
I do not think we need to spend too much time convincing anyone that there is a need in Canada for long-term agricultural credit. In its preliminary report the Gordon commission had this to say on page 28:
We believe that, in terms of farm income and the ability to service loans, the long-run prospects are favourable. Under these circumstances, farm credit agencies-
That would apply to the Canadian farm loan board.
-could appropriately extend the period of repayment up to 40 years for long-term loans-
In conclusion I should like to emphasize again what we in this group feel is necessary if the farm loan board is to serve the purpose it should. We feel that the amount of loan should be based on an increase from 65 per cent to 80 per cent of the appraised valuation. We feel also that the maximum amount of the loan should be increased from $15,000 to $20,000. We would ask the government to give serious consideration to reducing the interest rate charged on these loans.
Finally, we are asking for a new deal in connection with the appraisers of the farm loan board. We are asking that they become more liberal when appraising a property upon which a loan is being requested. We are asking also that the appraisals be uniform throughout western Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary assistant to the minister stated a few minutes ago that the rate of loans had been accelerated, and I feel that that will continue to be the case. The government now finds itself in the lending business and that being the case the man who would ordinarily lend money to a farmer will not lend it. He will tell the farmer to go to the farm loan board. In the few years I have been here I have done my best to assist the farm loan board.
When an applicant comes to me to see what I can do to help him get a loan, I try to help him. More than that, I go to the farm in question and value it myself. I find that the difficulty lies not so much in the fact that the percentage allowed is not high enough 

65 per cent is plenty in my opinion-but because very often the appraiser does not value the farm as he should. The appraiser goes along and puts the valuation on the farm that suits him, and I think there should be a tribunal set up so that in certain cases an

Canadian Farm Loan Act applicant may call in someone else and find what the farm is really worth. It is not the selling value of the farm that the appraiser takes into consideration, but his own valuation.
For example, just over a month ago I had a request from a man who had a mortgage on his farm of $2,500, secured on 100 acres of land with stock and buildings. As I understand it, he had borrowed this money from an old lady and she had reached the point where she needed the capital; the interest was not enough. The interest was paid up, but she wanted to close the mortgage. The farmer went to the farm loan board, but the valuer refused to give him a loan. All he asked for was $2,500 on 100 acres of land with stock and good buildings on it. The board, in this case, would have been taking no chance at all; the sum asked for was nowhere near the value of the property. I went to the loan board myself, but I have not heard what was done about the matter. This farmer could not get the money from a private lender. He had to go to the loan board as his only resort.
I think, also, that the government would be well advised to correct the form which applicants for loans are obliged to use. The forms are so complicated at present that the ordinary man does not understand them; it is necessary, almost, to have a lawyer in order to figure out what they mean. Farmers are dependent on this farm loan board, and the government might just as well acknowledge that if they are in the lending field they should look after these activities. If they are going to make the economy such that farmers are not allowed to make any money, they will have to do something else for them and make money a little easier to get.
I do not believe in mortgaging a farm for all it is worth; a man will only go down, that way. But after all there have been many cases where the board has refused to make loans it could have made to farmers who were not asking too much. Some of them are not asking for even half the price of their farms, and yet loans have been refused. I have interceded, myself, on behalf of some of these men, sometimes unsuccessfully. I think all of us should try to help these farm loan applicants because they cannot get help anywhere else, and I think the government should either get a little more liberal with their money or else change the name of their party.

Mr. Chairman, I propose to intervene only briefly in this discussion because I have to leave in a few minutes. I want to express my support of the views put forward by the hon. member for Kindersley. Those views represent the sentiments of all


hon. members of this group. I particularly wish to stress one point he raised, and that was that the board does not lend money to farmers to develop land upon which they do not reside. The hon. member explained the situation as it prevails in the prairie provinces, where farmers who are now living in villages and, in some cases, in towns, are quite suc-cesfully and efficiently farming land some distance away. I suppose that on the prairies they do that because of the greater convenience and the greater comfort gained.
The farmers in my constituency have frequently applied for loans on land on which they do not reside. In the case of the farmers whom I represent it is not a question of living in a village or in a small town; it is a question, usually, of living on one plot of land and farming one or more pieces of land at some distance from their homes. That, very often happens on account of local topography. To introduce a personal reference, I may say that I live at one spot and own various areas some miles away which are used for grazing cattle, and so on. But on the basis of the board's ruling in recent years, if I were to ask for a loan on a distant piece of property it would be refused because I do not reside on that property. That situation very frequently exists in our neighbourhood where, for instance, a farmer has a plot of land in the valley suitable for mixed farming and owns in addition a large hay-field on the uplands. I know one farmer who has such a field at 12 miles from his home; as a matter of fact it would be much better security for a loan than the land on which he actually resides and I do think that the present approach by officials of the board is an unfair one.
I urge that consideration should be given to granting applications for loans to farmers who wish to use those loans in the development of properties upon which they do not reside. I am not here to criticize the officials of the board as an organization or its officials in the provinces. I think that on the whole they are trying to do the best they can to administer the act efficiently and according to the terms of the legislation. However, I do think we must use a bit more imagination in the administration of farm credit in this country if it is going to fulfil its purpose-the development of an efficient agriculture and the development of the full potentiality of agriculture in Canada.
Some time during this session, if I remember correctly, the Prime Minister mentioned that there were large numbers of farmers in his province who were farming sub-marginal land. I would point out that this act does not provide any method by

which a farmer can transfer from submarginal land to good marginal land. I think we are bound to have an agricultural loan policy related to agriculture-a policy which co-ordinates the general policy of the government in respect to both agriculture and agricultural credit. The first aim should be to provide for loans for the efficient re-development of settled areas; second, the provision of loans for the development of new areas; and, third, for the lending of money for the purpose of transferring farmers now working marginal land to land upon which they could make a satisfactory living.
This would mean a considerable re-drafting of the act. In addition, I think something has to be done along the lines of the Veterans' Land Act. A young man with experience, often the son of a lifetime farmer, a man with good character but without capital should have the opportunity either to transfer from marginal land to good land, or to develop his older property, or to occupy unsettled land. I think there has to be a great deal more co-ordination between the various branches of the Department of Agriculture and also between the various branches of government with regard to agricultural credit in this country if it is to fulfil its purpose. There has to be co-ordination within the Department of Agriculture itself, and that department will have to co-ordinate its activities, in some cases with the forestry officials to get their opinion as to whether a certain farm may be situated on land which is sub-marginal and which would be better suited for the growing of trees, and so on; and provision made for transferring that farmer to suitable land elsewhere.
From the Atlantic to the Pacific in Canada we run into endless examples of people wasting their lives and their efforts on submarginal lands. We run into other cases where there could be a much more satisfactory redevelopment of good, occupied land. We also run into other cases where a lot of other first-rate agricultural land remains undeveloped because of the lack of co-ordination between various departments of government.
I shall never forget one occasion when I was fortunate enough to get a grant for clearing a river in my constituency involving the moving of log jams and things of that sort which caused the water level to rise in the spring and when it rose some 15,000 acres of land adjacent to the river were flooded. While the application was made in the first place to remove these log jams so as to improve navigation, the greater economic effect of their removal was to make it possible for the farmers to get on their land 82715-85
Canadian Farm Loan Act about three weeks earlier every spring. That was of great advantage to the farmers. But I was told that I must on no account mention the advantage obtained by the farmers in question or the public works department would not have the right to remove the log jams because the primary purpose of the removal of the log jams must be for navigation.
I mention that to indicate the lack of coordination at this time between various departments. Therefore I suggest that the time is approaching when we have got to face the question of agricultural credit with imagination if we are going to meet the needs of the people of Canada, particularly the young people who wish to farm, and if we are going to develop an efficient agriculture in this country.

The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose has set forth the stand of our group regarding the bill but I have one or two questions I should like to ask the minister. I understand he has prepared a statement for the hon. member for Greenwood showing the expansion in loans made by the farm loan board during the past few years. I wonder whether he could give me a statement at the same time showing the decrease in loans by private mortgage companies during the same period. At one time a lot of loans were made by private mortgage companies in the west but I understand that today they are practically out of business in that regard. I do not know whether any at all are being made. For that reason farmers today are practically dependent upon the farm loan board for any mortgages they may take on their lands. Apparently they cannot get any help from the private mortgage companies.
That being the case, it is well to note the fact that all farm organizations are complaining that the farm loan board is too conservative in its estimates of the value of land. The member for Battle River-Camrose mentioned the fact that he had found that the officials of the board were far more conservative than the Veterans' Land Act officials. In my district there have been strong complaints against the Veterans' Land Act officials that they were too conservative. If the farm loan board officials are even more conservative than the Veterans' Land Act officials, then they must indeed be very conservative.
I know that in my area, where land is of quite a high value, the Veterans' Land Act officials have been very conservative. There have been cases where, in the opinion of the farmers there based on what they could sell land for, $4,000 a quarter could have

Canadian Farm Loan Act been obtained for land but when it came to getting a loan the Veterans' Land Act officials only valued the land at around $2,000, or about 50 per cent of its actual value.
The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose pointed out that the application forms had been improved and simplified. That is true, but even so may I say that personally as a farmer I would refuse to sign such a form. I maintain there are certain things in the form that should not be there. No farmer should be asked to sign such a form and I will explain why. First of all, on page 1 the applicant is told to read page 4 before making out the application form. I think that is very good advice because if you have got any sense you will not sign the form after reading page 4. On page 4 there is the following.
I make this application for loan subject to the following conditions:
1.	That the application fee will be refunded if an appraisal is not made but will be retained by the board if an appraisal is made whether or not my application is approved.
I have no objection to that. Then we come to No. 2, and I take strong exception to it. It reads:
2.	That I will execute a mortgage on the board's form as a first charge on said lands as security for the amount of loan granted by the board, and if required a chattel mortgage on all or such of my goods, chattels, livestock and machinery as may be specified by the board as additional security for such loan and will pay all fees and disbursements incurred by the board in the investigation of title and the perfecting thereof, and I hereby charge the said lands with the payment of such costs. I hereby agree that, notwithstanding the execution or registration of the mortgage or mortgages, the advancing of the money or any part thereof shall at all times be in the absolute discretion of the board.
It is charged by farm organizations and, I think, by everyone who is familiar with the act, that the board is too conservative in the valuation of land. But, not content with that, the board has the right to demand that the farmer sign a chattel mortgage on everything else that he possesses.

Everything except his wife. I do not know whether or not they have gone that far. I hope not. I would ask the minister what would be the credit position of a farmer if he agreed to sign a chattel mortgage on everything else that he possessed. What would be his credit standing at the bank if he wanted a short term loan and if, when asked by the bank manager to give a statement, he indicated that everything he had was covered by a chattel mortgage to the farm loan board? I think hon. members will agree that his


credit standing would be nil. The only chance he would have to get any loan at all would be entirely upon the basis of his character. A man's character is not sufficient for him to get a loan if conditions are bad and there is not much chance of his being able to repay the loan, not because he does not desire to do so, not because he is not honest but just because he has signed over everything to the farm loan board. I think that provision certainly should be limited.
You may say that this is merely an application and if at the time the loan is to be disbursed he refuses to sign the form he is still no worse off because he does not have to take the loan. But look at section 4. It reads:
4. That if after approval of this application I fail upon request after notification of such approval to execute any documents deemed necessary by the board to complete the security, I will pay all expenses incurred by the board in the consideration of the application and in the investigation of title.
So he signs the application form and then is told later that he has got to give a chattel mortgage on everything he possesses. Naturally if the farmer has any sense at all he will refuse to do so. But then he has to pay any expenses incurred even though he is not going to get the loan. I should like the minister to tell us on how many occasions farmers have been required to sign chattel mortgages. Maybe the minister can say that it has never been done. If it has never been done, I think that is pretty good evidence it is really not necessary to have that provision in there and I think the minister certainly should give consideration to modifying it.
There is one other thing I do not like in the form. Section 7 reads:
7. I hereby authorize and request the board to remit the balance of loan or loans granted to me by cheque, payable to the order of myself ... by mail at my risk . . .
Why should it be at the applicant's risk? If I owe somebody a debt and mail that person a cheque and the cheque is lost, I am the one who has to stand the loss or straighten out the matter. The person to whom I send the cheque does not have to stand the loss, so why should the farmer stand the loss if he never gets the cheque? It seems to me that if the farm loan board took proper precautions there would be no risk involved of the farmer not receiving the money, and I fail to understand why the words "at my risk" should be inserted in there. It is just one other thing that may scare off the farmers. I hope the minister can give us a satisfactory explanation with regard to section 2.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the farm loan board has not kept pace

with general developments in agriculture. I find myself very much in agreement with much that has been said today, and in particular what the hon. member for Huron has said is so true. The man on the farm today has to spend a lot more money in setting up his farm. Young men starting farms today are spending many times what was spent a few years ago. The cost of machinery, the cost of livestock, the cost of operation of the farm has very little in common with the cost of 25 or 30 years ago. Perhaps this farm loan board has been directed by the government to be careful and it would be only recklessness to suggest that they should make loans to 90 per cent of the value of the farm, but, on the other hand, I do not think the function of this lending body should be to be so careful that they have a large surplus every year.
As the hon. member for Huron has said, you are in the lending business and the fact you have a Canadian farm loan board makes it almost impossible for a young farmer to get money anywhere else. This is especially true in view of the tight money policy the government now has, and when the banks are told not only to increase interest rates to unprecedented heights but to restrict the credit of a farmer who wants to build a barn in spite of the fact he may have good collateral. There never has been a time when farmers were more hampered in their production plans than they are now. I am not going to review the number of farmers who are operating under great difficulties. I know, Mr. Chairman, that almost every hon. member in this house who is familiar with rural conditions in Canada is well aware that there are a great many farmers who are finding it difficult now. Even the Prime Minister has been talking about marginal farms, and when he gets into that field he will find the marginal area is pretty wide today.
In connection with the limiting of the value of a farm to $15,000, I might point out to the parliamentary assistant that that sounded like a lot of money a few years ago. At that time the government was spending only around $500 million and now it is spending $5,000 million. In those days a farmer knew he could buy a binder for $125, but today he pays $800 for one. These are two different eras.

Not the same dollars, either.
The same thing could be said of almost every aspect of farm equipment. He has more money invested in his livestock, his 82715-85J
Canadian Farm Loan Act dairy cattle; everything on the farm is costing a lot more money. I do not believe this factor has been taken into account by the farm loan board.
Another factor that is not taken into account by the board is the replacement cost of farm buildings. Buildings do not have to burn down to need replacement. They need repair, such as new roofs and so forth. You know very well that it costs as much today to put a roof on a barn as it did to build the barn 30 years ago. These are factors the farmer is up against. As the hon. member for Huron has so well said, the farmer cannot go and borrow as he could years ago. There are some who might say when your party was in power you had the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and that hurt credit to a certain amount in those difficult days. The fact is, however, that we must be up to date if we are going to do business. The farm loan board should keep up with the times and pay attention to these essential factors. They should realize that the farmer has not got the same opportunity of borrowing money he used to have. He does not go to the old retired farmer who had $10,000 or $15,000 that he was glad to put out in mortgages at 5 per cent. The retired farmer would say now, why don't you go to the farm loan board; we have a Canadian farm loan board. Well, I have been to them and I cannot get it. If you only need that much money, you have a lot of stock and implements so why don't you go to the bank? The bank has been told by the head of the Bank of Canada that they are not to lend any more.
I know of cases where banks have refused to lend a farmer money, even though in my opinion his collateral looked good. If you want to help in this inflationary period, I think it is just as important to encourage production as it is to try to restrict credit. Certainly this is more important in helping inflation than increasing the handouts from the government which do not result in production. Often the valuator comes and tells the farmer he is not doing this or that right. He looks at the farmer, sizes him up to see-whether he shaved that day or the day before^ whether he has a smart looking wife who is a good housekeeper; whether things look shipshape and painted, and then he says this looks pretty good. He goes to another place where the farmer has been too busy to shave for two or three days but who is making, more money than the first fellow and often the investigator does not know whether he is looking at a Jersey cow or a Holstein, but he refuses the farmer a loan. I know of cases in which a farmer has wanted a loan of 65 per cent of the value of a good farm. The

Canadian Farm Loan Act valuator has said they could not give that much on that farm; he did not believe it was worth that much. The farmer says, I was offered $12,000 for it and all I am asking is 65 per cent of $10,000 but you say it is not worth that much. I wish I had sold it. These may be extreme cases, but we have all heard of them.
The objective of the farm loan board seems to be not to get into trouble, not to lend too much for fear they might lose a little. I do not like to see the government acting recklessly in any department, but the lack of caution I see in some of the expenditures by this government amazes me when it is contrasted with the caution exhibited by the farm loan board. I know that in my own county many farmers have been refused loans which appear to be within the close range of good security for the farm loan board. They were refused merely because the owner of the farm, a young man, was energetic enough to try to supplement his income at a period when costs are rising and prices falling; at a time when agriculture is getting a smaller share of the national income per capita than any other industry in Canada. The farmer is refused a loan because he is energetic enough to go for two or three months a year and earn a salary at Camp Borden or Malton airport. The inspector tells him he can make more money at home. This government tries to tell you how to spend your own money. You are supposed to spend less yourself while they spend more all the time.
The inspector tells this young farmer he could make more money at home. The farmer says, doing what? I have not enough money to buy more milk cows. The tight money policy of the government will not allow the bank to lend me money to supplement my production by purchasing four or five more cows at a cost of $1,200. He has a choice then. He can either let the farm go and take his wife and family into town, quit farming altogether, or he can continue to take his job. Often he finds that with good wages he can afford to choose the latter. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, therefore, that good administration by the board would not be so greatly concerned with the letter of the law.
I hope the government will urge the farm loan board to be a little more lenient. I am not blaming the personnel of the farm loan board. I think it is a lack of appreciation by the government itself of the real problems of agriculture at this time. I think they should risk a little more. If you are in the lending business and getting good interest you should lend money.
Another feature is this, Mr. Chairman. The sum of $15,000 may seem to some who talk

about farms being worth $8,000, $10,000 and $12,000 per 100 acres of land to be a lot of money; but there is another factor that every member who is familiar at all with agricultural problems is conscious of. Today, in very many instances, it is much more econom-i-al to run a large farm than a small one. In other words, the machinery involved in modern agriculture today is so costly that the farmer decides the larger unit is more important and more economical. I think it is. In many instances he is farming in an area near to a large city such as the suburban areas of Toronto or Montreal, or any of the large cities throughout Canada, and the large industrial centres and suburban districts. The farms in those districts are worth a lot more money. I think the farm loan board should be given leeway to lend more than $15,000.
I should like to know who is afraid of the farm loan board losing our dollars which this government takes from us so freely and handles so recklessly. Who is there amongst us who thinks that you could not lend more than $15,000 on some of the 100-acre farms within say 25 miles or 30 miles of Toronto or Montreal, if it is good producing land? If it is 300 or 400 miles back from those districts its production value would be just as good as far as the soil is concerned but its actual value would be less. Because land is close to the Toronto or Montreal markets its earning capacity is greater. Regardless of that, Mr. Chairman, if a farmer's loan is increased and he should fail the farm loan board would not lose any money.
As the parliamentary assistant knows, good land in proximity to those big cities is selling from $300 to $500 an acre. Therefore, in my opinion, the $15,000 limit is outmoded. To raise the $15,000 limit does not mean that the farm loan board is going to be reckless and that they will lend it in a different way from what they are doing now. But, there are extreme cases. I think the farm loan board could be a good deal more use than it is.
I notice that they have not lost much money but they have not lent much money. Today the farmers are up against great difficulties. Their costs are rising and their income is lower. Land values have increased, the cost of machinery has increased and replacement costs have increased. If a roof blows off a barn, if a barn blows down, if it does not burn, very often the cost of replacement is a great deal more than it used to be. The whole administration of the farm loan board should be encouraged to give more loans and increase the limit under these changing conditions and either be in the lending business or not. Because of the tight

We hope that agricultural conditions will improve. Nevertheless, I believe there are many farmers who have gone out of business because of the tight-money planning of the farm loan board. I believe they could have taken a little more risk and they would have lost very little if anything, and our national economy could have been more usefully served.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say one or two words on this particular act. This morning the parliamentary assistant pointed out that the main purpose of the bill is to increase the scope and facilities of the Canadian farm loan board. I am sure that hon. members of all parties will be in sympathy with this objective, because many of the troubles facing agriculture today can certainly be traced to the lack of long-term farm credit. I feel that this lack has caused real trouble in most of our farming communities.
In the first place, many of our young farmers who would like to stay on the land, have been forced to go into the cities, because they cannot find enough money to establish themselves on the land.
In the second place, the lack of farm credit is causing a concentration of farms in the hands of wealthier people, because they, after all, are the ones who can most easily obtain any credit that is available. In the third place, I think the lack of adequate farm credit today in Canada is lowering the productivity of Canadian farms.
The reason for this undesirable situation is not very hard to find. Today private lenders, whether they be banks, mortgage companies or insurance companies, can find more lucrative and less risky fields in which to put their money. As a result, in latter years those companies have been placing an ever smaller amount of their investment funds into farm mortgages. I think the recent actions of the Bank of Canada have aggravated the farm credit problem, and thus, as never before, we are in the position today where the farmers must depend upon the Canadian farm loan board to give them long-term credit.
There are two special and additional reasons, Mr. Chairman, why today the farmers of Saskatchewan need some kind of additional assistance. Back in the depression years we had a great many farm foreclosures by mortgage companies. A lot of us felt that many of these foreclosures were unwarranted. In 1944 the Saskatchewan C.C.F.
Canadian Farm Loan Act government introduced a bill called the Saskatchewan moratorium act. I think it was introduced in good faith. The effect of the legislation was to prevent foreclosure on the home quarter. I admit quite frankly that I supported this legislation at the time, because I thought it was a good thing for the farmers. Unfortunately it has not worked out that way, in my opinion. The mortgage companies, feeling that they no longer had any security of investment in the province of Saskatchewan after that act was passed, pulled out lock, stock and barrel. Thus in my opinion, this legislation has had the-effect of virtually ruining farm credit in the province of Saskatchewan; because even though the Supreme Court ultimately ruled it ultra vires, the companies have not come back into the province.
The C.C.F. government took another step which I think has harmed farm credit In the province of Saskatchewan. For many years, under a Liberal administration, we had out there a provincial farm loan board. It made loans to farmers at low interest rates. Yet one of the first acts of the C.C.F. government in 1944 was to repeal the Saskatchewan farm loan act and abolish the board. Today the C.C.F. government, which professes to have such a great interest in the farmer, refuses to loan him even a five-cent piece. That is why this legislation before us today is so important to the Saskatchewan farmer, Mr. Chairman.
Under the Canadian Farm Loan Act which was passed back in 1927 the federal government lends money to farmers for all general farm purposes. Since its inception it has lent $25,500,000 out in my province, and for a number of years I am told, in this house prairie Liberal members have been urging the government to extend its provisions and make more money available. If I understood the parliamentary assistant correctly, an additional $20 million will now be made available for farm credit. This is a tangible measure introduced by the Liberal government which will be of genuine assistance to Canadian farmers.
My hon. friends in the C.C.F. party both in Saskatchewan and out in the hustings from time to time have disparaged the value of the Canadian farm loan board. For instance, if I may paraphrase his words, the hon. member for Kindersley said this morning that the policy of the board seemed to be "as stingy as possible." The socialists say that loans are too difficult to obtain, interest rates are excessive, the amount which the board will loan is too small, and so on. I say that it ill becomes a group which has done

Canadian Farm Loan Act so little to provide the farmer of Saskatchewan with long term credit, to criticize a resolution of this kind.
We appreciate that these amendments are not going to completely solve the problem, but they are certainly a step in the right direction. I say flatly that this resolution should be supplemented by provincial legislation in every province which does not already have a provincial farm loan act. If the socialists are sincere in their concern for the farmers I think they should persuade their colleagues back in Saskatchewan to reintroduce legislation establishing a farm loan board, such as formerly existed under the Liberal administration. It seems to me that instead of constantly telling the federal government what it should be doing, the socialists themselves should take some useful and practical action which will help the farmers.
Today there are a number of provinces which have provincial farm loan boards. For example, Quebec has a board which loans money at an interest rate of 2J per cent, and it is loaned for a period of up to 39J years. A few weeks ago I wrote the director and asked him to tell me something about the Quebec act. He wrote me as follows:
The results have been wonderful until now. As we are writing you, we have granted loans to the extent of $140 million and the present session has voted an additional amount of $15 million.
I have heard many of my socialist friends describe the government of Premier Duplessis as reactionary and backward. Although I do not choose to become involved in that kind of discussion today, I will say this. The Quebec farm loan board act is so far ahead of anything which has been provided by the socialists in Saskatchewan, that it almost reflects on the sincerity of the socialists toward agriculture.
I understand there is a farm loan act in existence in Ontario under which money is loaned to young farmers at 4 per cent. It appears to me to be a fairly good act. As I listened to some opposition members from Ontario speaking I wondered why they are not urging their own provincial farm loan board to extend its operations.
On the prairies the socialists are forever telling people that they are the champions of the farmer. The C.C.F. members incessantly talk about the needs of the farmers, yet in Saskatchewan where they form the government, as far as I can see, they do practically nothing for agriculture. The resolution before us today is one more example of Liberal legislation which will be of valuable assistance to the farmers.
I wish to conclude by throwing out a challenge to the C.C.F. I say to them, let us have


action instead of words. If you really believe that the farmers of Saskatchewan should be provided with better long-term credit facilities, emulate the example set by other provincial governments and by former Liberal governments in Saskatchewan, and reconstitute the Saskatchewan farm loan board. Then and only then will the criticism which you are making today cease to sound empty and hollow. I believe that these amendments are progressive and will benefit the farmers of Canada. They have my wholehearted support.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word not concerning the administration of the board but with regard to two matters which came up in the banking and commerce committee last year. The first related to the length of time taken in servicing the applications for loans. There was a great deal of discussion about this matter and I would like some information concerning it. I would be grateful if the parliamentary assistant would provide us with information indicating whether or not there has been an improvement with respect to the length of time involved in servicing applications. I should also like to have a statement showing the amount of business that has been done by the board over the last several years so that we will have an idea of the volume of business they handle.

Mr. Chairman, it is amazing to hear so many of the free enterprisers in this house welcome this resolution. It is quite a common thing that when free enterprise fails, then the government and the taxpayers are supposed to come to the rescue.
The sincerity of the members of this group was called into question a few moments ago when we plead for an extension of facilities for farm credit. There are a great many people in Canada who learned long ago that there is more money to be made when you farm the farmer than when you farm the land.
The parliamentary assistant made a rather important statement in his opening remarks when he said there has been an accelerated demand. If that accelerated demand reflects the heightened desire of the Canadian farm loan board to supply long-term credit for Canadian agriculture then of course that statement is to be welcomed. However, if the accelerated demand has been caused by the poor economic conditions of Canadian agriculture then it is a reflection that is most undesirable.
What I have reference to when I say that is the statement in the annual report dealing with the purposes for which loans have been made during the past year. It says that 30.1 per cent of the loans were made for the

purpose of paying off debts. I think the committee will recall that a year ago when we were debating the bill limiting interest rates charged by finance companies it was revealed that half of the total number of loans that had been made in one year by the finance companies were made to people who wanted to pay off loans they had already made. In other words, half the money was being used to help people refinance their debts. I regret very much that Canadian agriculture has reached the state of affairs where 30 per cent of the mortgages have to be used to pay off debts. I would much rather see a higher percentage of the loans devoted to the cause of increasing the productivity of these farms.
Progress reported.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Chairman, when we closed last night I was discussing the dangers which are imminent in respect of the activities of UNESCO. It is not my intention to occupy much more of the time of the committee just now, but I do believe that there are some other considerations which ought to be placed before the committee before we leave this discussion. For the sake of those who may pick up today's Hansard without having gone through the Hansard of yesterday it might be wise to review briefly what UNESCO is and indicate two or three important facts concerning its development.
First of all, what is the meaning of UNESCO? The word UNESCO is made up of the first letters of six words, namely United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organization. What can be said about the beginnings of UNESCO? The United Nations charter signed in San Francisco on June 26, 1945 included a provision for the promotion of cultural and educational co-operation between the member states.
Canada Council
The first conference for establishing an educational and cultural organization was convened in London in November 1945 and the representatives of the participating nations signed the constitution of UNESCO on November 15, 1945. The constitution of UNESCO entered into force on November 4, 1946. The acceptance of membership in UNESCO by the United States was authorized by public law 565 adopted at the second session of the 79th congress on July 30, 1946. This gives us a sort of passing bird's eye view of the general picture bringing it up to the point when the UNESCO commission of the United States was first established. I dealt with that event yesterday in the opening of my remarks.
Yesterday I devoted a considerable amount of attention to establishing the fact that the UNESCO program in the United States and presumably elsewhere where it was in operation was seeking definitely by propaganda to destroy patriotism in youth, to dispense with religion, to belittle parents and diminish their influence over their children, and finally to neglect a grounding in the three R's presumably so that when children grew up they would not have the ability to interpret the printed page and consequently would not be able to comprehend very clearly what was written in any document which to any extent was complex. What a calamity that would be to a nation like the United States requires only a moment's reflection to realize.
There are one or two additional things I wish to mention today. I am going to refer to a periodical which I have always found for many years to be reliable. This is called The American Nationalist, and the number to which I propose to refer is the November 1954 issue. Hon. members who will take pains to consult this particular number of this periodical will find on page 1 a headline "UNESCO Joins Segregation Fight". Hon. members will wonder what possible connection there can be between segregation and education and culture. This refers particularly to the United States.
On page 3 there is a headline "UNESCO pushes desegregation in the United States". It is almost beyond the power of imagination in a nightmare to conceive what possible connection there could be between culture and education, the arts and humanities and social sciences and all these other pretty decorations we have been talking about, and desegregation in the United States.

Those who will be reading these remarks of mine in the country and those who are listening in this house will, I think, - be greatly impressed if they follow closely just what these words are and what they imply:
Conclusion. Supposedly UNESCO is an organization devoted to the furtherance of educational, scientific and cultural advancement. The most logical place for its activities would therefore seem to be in the more backward areas of the world where there is a crying need for educational and scientific improvement. But UNESCO is not filling that need; instead it chooses to lavish its attentions upon Americans, who already have one of the world's best education systems.
This preoccupation with the educational and cultural well-being of the American people would be most flattering were it not for the type of "culture" and "education" involved. Actually, of course, it is neither education nor culture; it is propaganda.
And in this connection I will refer hon. members to the quotation I made from Senator McCarran in my remarks last night. From the excerpt "Conclusion" I continue to read:
Furthermore it is propaganda designed to prepare the Americans for world government; propaganda which is frankly directed toward the destruction of our patriotism-
This refers to the United States.
-and racial self respect.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: There's bigotry for you.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I will leave the hon. member to talk with the editor of this periodical, and I recommend him to take a course in a lot of things he does not know much about before he undertakes it.
At this point a pertinent' question is, why this concentration on the United States? I suggest the reason is this-that the masterminds of the world revolutionary movement to whom I referred last night realize that the strongest bastion of human freedom of the world is the United States. They know that if they can bring down the United States, and bring it under a world dictatorship, they will have achieved t'heir purpose throughout the world. That is the reason behind this concentration on the United States. And now that they have the United States pretty well ready to fall into their hands they are going to turn their attention to Canada because here again is a bastion of human freedom, and if they can get the United States and Canada away from the British commonwealth-away from Great Britain-I need not even hint what would be the result for the free peoples of the world.

I go on now to quote one further paragraph from the article "Conclusion" from which I have quoted:
It is high time the United States put a stop to this flood of alien racist agitation. The question of whether or not we are to have segregation in our armed forces and in our public schools is one for Americans to decide-not foreigners. No foreign agency-UNESCO or any other-should be allowed to intercede on either side of the question. For that reason UNESCO should be compelled to halt the distribution of all literature within the United States which advocates de-segregation or which, indirectly or otherwise, attacks those who uphold segregation.
Let me once more point out to those who are present in the house and to those who will read this in the country how dreadfully serious every phase in that passage is, not only in its meaning but in its implication. I think I will say no more at the present time in respect of this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to delay the committee for very long. However, after listening to the "fountain of knowledge" for some considerable time I feel that a number of things were said against the work of UNESCO which need at least some repudiation.
I have had personal observation of only one phase of the work that is being conducted by that organization. The hon. member for Macleod assured this house some time ago that he believed UNESCO was an "evil thing". I think those were his exact words. I attended a dinner some time ago at which the guest speaker was one of the leading educationists in the city of Ottawa and he had brought along with him moving pictures of the work that he had done for UNESCO for several years.
We all know that hundreds of thousands of Arab refugees live in the Gaza strip. The outlook in the world today for these refugees looks very black indeed. It is obvious that most of the countries of the world do not wish to admit these refugees as immigrants. Even when our own Minister of Citizenship and Immigration agreed to accept some of them he laid down very severe limitations respecting who would and would not be
Canada Council
admitted. One limitation he imposed had to do with the educational qualifications of would-be immigrants.
UNESCO is offering to these refugees the only educational facilities available to them. It is providing public schools as well as some high schools. UNESCO is assisting these helpless people whose only hope for the future is that maybe some civilized country will admit them if they obtain an education. If it is said that UNESCO is an evil thing when it undertakes projects of that kind, then I cannot disagree more.
As for the comments of the hon. member for Lethbridge, I do not think that the work of UNESCO should be limited only to those areas of the world that he or I might choose to designate as less than civilized. I am quite prepared to admit that even the people of Canada or the people of the United States could stand a little bit of education in certain respects. If UNESCO does engage in efforts to break down racial prejudice throughout the world, if UNESCO attempts to persuade the white people of the United States to be a little more cultured and civilized, if in Canada it should attempt to persuade us that maybe the Indian is a worthy Canadian citizen and deserving of the same rights and privileges as the white man, then I say three cheers for UNESCO and UNESCO is worthy of our support.
