speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. The statute provides that the chairman of the Canada Council and one other member appointed by the council will belong to the investment committee and there will be three others. It is intended that they will be persons chosen from outside the council to act with the other two as an advisory body on the selection of the investments to be made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Within that framework, I wonder if the Prime Minister would consider a suggested addition to this clause to take care of something which is needed. The Canada Council has the life on the council of each of its members limited to three years. At the end of that time they may be reappointed for another term. We have a provision here for the establishment of an investment committee.
[Mr. St. Laurent (Quebec East) .1
The life on the committee of the three persons appointed by the governor in council is indefinite. It would seem to me conceivable that at some point this could be a source of some embarrassment. The members of the body would grow older as the years went by and perhaps they might be taken sick. Although I hope this would never be the case, it may be that over a period of years there would be some cause to question the continuing judgment of some of the members. It also may be that a person appointed to such a body with a given set of business connections would change his business connections in such a way as to render him less valuable to the investment committee. These are factors which at some point might cause the government to wish to see someone dropped from the investment committee. It is a foreseeable situation. If there is no provision in the act whereby these appointments come up periodically for review it puts the government in the embarrassing position of having to approach someone and suggest they retire.
The amendment which I have in mind would not obligate the government to change the nature of the investment committee at any given period of time because it stipulates that the members may be reappointed. This would give the government complete freedom to continue its membership on the same basis and with the same personnel if so desired. On the other hand the amendment I intend to propose establishes the periodic review of the personnel of this committee and it would allow for any necessary changes to be made with a minimum of embarrassment.
Having said that Mr. Chairman, I would therefore move to amend clause 18 by adding after subclause 3 two subclauses as follow:
To amend section 18 by adding after subsection (3) :
"(4) Each of the members of the investment committee appointed by the governor in council under the provisions of section 18	(1) of this
act shall be appointed for a term of three years except that of those first appointed one shall be appointed for a term of two years, one shall be appointed for a term of three years, and one shall be appointed for a term of four years.	,
(5) A person appointed under the provisions of section 18 (4) of this act shall be eligible for reappointment."
Before I resume my seat I should like to point out that I have tried in proposing this amendment to follow the same terminology used in connection with the Canada Council itself at the beginning of the bill, that is to have a rotating committee on which one member would come up each year for reappointment. The committee would remain the same for the first two years which would give a measure of continuity in the beginning, but the term of any one member once

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: the committee was in operation would not exceed three years before he became subject to review as a continuing member of the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there can be no serious objection to the requirement of looking at the appointments every three years to see if they are still in order. It must not be forgotten that this is an advisory committee and it would perhaps be something that would make the members of the committee feel a sense of somewhat greater responsibility if they knew that they might be there for quite a long period and have the wisdom or unwisdom of their selections of investments appear while they were still members of the committee. It is quite possible to have an investment look very good for two or three years and then after eight or ten years not look quite so good. That has happened to me in connection with the small investments I have had to make from time to time.
If the committee feels that this is something that would make for sounder administration then there would be no other objection than the one I have formulated because the amendment does provide that the government can re-appoint the gentleman or lady in question if it seems proper to do so. But it does seem to me it would be well to clarify the situation of this advisory committee. I think it was felt that there would be an advisory committee that would not have a permanent membership but which would acquire experience that would be added to the experience which a particular appointee might have, which would all be added to the acquired experience of the committee and thus be of value to the council.
If the hon. gentleman puts his amendment I would ask every hon. member in the committee to vote in the manner that would appear to him to make for the best results for the Canada Council because it seems to me that the desirability or otherwise of the amendment is pretty evenly balanced.

Mr. Chairman, I think that is a very fair and reasonable approach on the part of the Prime Minister but I do want to say a couple of words because it seems to me that even he might be persuaded to come along with the amendment. Perhaps I should draw to his attention the fact that members of the Canada Council after their second term of appointment are specifically precluded from being re-appointed for a period of twelve months. In drafting this amendment I carefully moved away from that because of my
Canada Council
realization that what the legislation had in mind was a continuing body.
The point that the Prime Minister made, that an investment may not look good after six or eight years, is something that I think gives strong support to this amendment. Let us imagine that they do not look very good at the end of six or eight years. Surely if that has been a consistent pattern on the part of the committee no one would want to continue with that same investment group nor would they want to face the embarrassment, unless they had to, of going to them and saying, "We wish you would resign". I am grateful to the Prime Minister for indicating that this amendment deserves attention and I propose to leave it at that.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to venture to ask the Prime Minister if perhaps he could not accept this amendment. My colleague has paid him the compliment of keeping close to the plan of appointment set out in clause 4 and has made it clear by the provision for re-appointment that he does not intend standing in the way of the Prime Minister's idea that we need a long period of service here in order to get the best results. In other words, I think my colleague is trying to help rather than to obstruct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sure he is, and that is why I am suggesting that all hon. members wherever they may sit should bring their own judgment to bear upon the advisability or otherwise of agreeing to this amendment. I have no firm opinion about it. I know that there could arise situations where it would be convenient to have a termination date, but whether that convenience would outweigh the advantages of making appointments to last during pleasure or not is something about which I have no firm opinion.
Will the members of this committee receive a salary or a per diem remuneration? Is it to be a permanent part of the council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there might be an honorarium paid for services rendered. It might well be that one member of the committee would be asked to make a special investigation into a certain number of securities and would receive an honorarium for doing that work without a similar honorarium being paid to other members of the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Like some other members of this committee I am trying to balance the arguments for and against this proposal. If the amendment moved by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace does not carry, and if clause 18 in its original form is enacted,

Canada Council
how do these other three members get "unappointed"? Are they appointed tor life?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They will get "unappointed" by someone else being appointed in their stead. I am told the question has arisen on several occasions in connection with the civil service. It is not necessary to have a person resign. If someone is appointed to the office he holds, in his stead, that amounts to a demotion, and the new appointee takes the place of the old.
That is what they call "bumping".

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It may be
called "bumping", but it is the effect of placing a new appointee in the position that is occupied by the one who becomes his predecessor, and there are occasions when it is a convenience in the civil service to have statutory provisions that require retirement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before the Prime Minister made his last remarks, Mr. Chairman, I was leaning slightly against the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, but now I am leaning slightly the other way.
Make up your mind.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What bothers me about the amendment moved by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace is that it seems to me you could have a situation where one member of the committee would be re-appointed at the end of his term while another would not; and you would have a feeling of discrimination. But now the Prime Minister tells us that if such an amendment is not adopted the members will stay on the committee until they are replaced by someone else being appointed-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Or until they resign, or ask to be relieved.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But the Prime Minister also said that even if there were no resignations a person might be replaced by someone else being appointed in his stead.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It seems to me that the arrangement explained by the Prime Minister leaves something of a vacuum-that it would leave us without any regular way of handling this situation, and I think I am leaning a little more toward the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace.

It seems to me that the Prime Minister has been very fair and reasonable in his suggestions, but I think the motion of the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace has quite a deal of merit in it, and I cannot

help but think it would be less embarrassing, and probably better for the general efficiency of the scheme, if some term of years could be mentioned. If the members of the committee were all satisfactory, they could naturally be re-appointed. The Prime Minister has mentioned that new members would be appointed should a vacancy arise through a resignation or, naturally, through death, but it is quite conceivable that no matter how good the appointees are it might be decided after a few years of trial and error that someone else could fill a certain place better, and I would hope, as the hon. member for Greenwood has said, that the Prime Minister might accept the amendment, or that the house should accept it at least, because the present arrangement does appear to me to contain possibilities of embarrassment. As I said, the members might prove to be not as efficient as was anticipated, and I think the setting of the term of years would be an improvement.

I apologize for speaking again, but I have had a somewhat similar experience to that of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I had already intended to vote for my colleague's amendment, but as I thought it over I began to find what I believe is a better argument. Also, it is a very interesting possibility that with a free vote one might actually change some members' votes by one's words.
This is my point. It seems to me, if you look at it in a practical way, that when an appointment is made without a time limit it is virtually an appointment for life. It is almost offensive if you go to a man and ask him to retire, that is, if he is able to walk unaided, and looks reasonably intelligent. This does not seem to me to be a good thing, especially in view of the wide open investment powers contained under the act-powers which I shall, incidentally, be asking the committee to consider and revise at a later stage. As the position stands now we are appointing three men to invest a large amount of money, and they will have wide open powers; they can invest in anything.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They can advise the council. The council is not obliged to follow the advice given, but it will have the benefit of that advice, and, as the hon. gentleman says, that can cover anything in the field of investment.

Well, I take it you will have on this investment committee some presumably expert investors, if there are any, and on the other hand you will have on the council gentlemen who are not supposed to

be good investors, though I have seen university professors who can invest better than stockbrokers. But in view of that situation it seems to me there is a great deal to be said for not having these men appointed without a time limit being set. Suppose you appoint two or three men, and they make some mistakes, and, as the Prime Minister has indicated, after a few years the investments do not look so good? What would be the position then? I suggest there is a good deal of merit in having these positions up for review at the end of a definite time, at which point changes could be made without offence. If these men are appointed without any time limit it would be almost an affront, while they still enjoyed full vigour and capacity, to ask any of them to retire.
Amendment (Mr. Hamilton, Notre Dame de Grace) negatived: Yeas, 22; nays, 41.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost.

I should like to say one more thing in connection with this section. Subsection (3) provides for payment or remuneration to members of the investment committee, and states:
The members of the investment committee appointed by the governor in council may be paid for their services such remuneration and expenses as are fixed by the governor in council.
It does not state by whom they are to be paid. This, again, may be covered by the Interpretation Act, but I think we might know whether this remuneration is to be paid by the Canada Council or by the treasury.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will look back to section 16 he will see that any expenditure made for any of the purposes of this act, except section 9, may be paid out of the income of the endowment fund.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 19-Property.

This clause provides that the council may hold and dispose of real and personal property and, subject to any other provision of the act and on the advice of the investment committee, may invest in any manner it sees fit any money standing to the credit of the endowment fund or the university capital grants fund, and so on. I was surprised-I will not use a stronger word- to see these wide-open powers of investment given. Two clauses later the council is described as a charitable organization. I think the Prime Minister will agree with me that in the case of charitable organizations there is nearly always an investment restriction. I do not know whether he will agree
Canada Council
with the statement I make, but I have known of a fair number of charitable organizations and I have not known of one where there were wide-open powers of investment as there are here.
I think we want to be quite clear in our minds as to what this means. This means that if the investment committee advises and the council approves there is no reason why this huge amount of money could not all be invested in oil stocks, let us say.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Pardon?

I say there is no reason why all this money could not be invested in oil stocks. The Prime Minister does not disagree. Unless there is some reason for it, that I have not been able to imagine, which could conceivably change the situation, it seems to me that this is an extraordinary proposition. I believe one leading newspaper welcomed this provision because they said it meant the council would be able to grow up with the country and share in the benefits of the increased value of what are called growth stocks.
A few minutes ago I thought the Prime Minister characterized the situation very well. He said that in connection with stock investments you sometimes get into things which look very good and then you find they are not so good. But my point is, what is the reason for departing from what I think the Prime Minister will agree is almost a universal rule viz that when you have charitable or trust funds there shall be some restriction? The restriction I am going to suggest is that this council should have the same investment powers as insurance companies. The Prime Minister will know all about that.
That does not mean you have to invest everything in Dominion of Canada bonds, as is provided earlier for reasons which the Prime Minister made clear, but it does mean that you are restricted. You can invest 15 per cent, I think it is, in common stocks; but they must be common stocks that have a good dividend record, and so on. I need not go into the details. First of all, having regard to the fact that this is a charitable trust, does the Prime Minister agree that this is an unusual provision? Second, will he explain to us, if he agrees that it is unusual, why this provision is being put in here?

May I also add my words to those of the member for Greenwood. I was going to raise exactly the same point. I am a director of an educational trust fund in the province of British Columbia, and we are very much governed by the laws of the province and the dominion as to how we can invest our funds. The government is very

Canada Council
careful to check not less than once a year on how our funds are being invested and administered. I agree almost completely with the restriction imposed by legislation upon those in charge of such funds that they can only make certain investments.
As I understand the bill, this is a trust fund and the moneys are either coming from the taxpayers of Canada through the government of Canada or from endowments made under a certain clause of the bill. Because it is to be considered a council for charitable purposes under the Income Tax Act, I fail completely to see how it differs in any way, in the administration of the funds of an absolute trust, from any other organization administering trust funds and completely governed by acts of parliament as to how they can invest their money.
As an administrator of a large trust fund in British Columbia I find myself wondering why in clause 19 authority is given to the council, on the advice of the investment committee, to invest its funds in any way it sees fit. For as many years as I can remember the government of Canada has insisted that trust moneys can only be invested in a certain manner. Now you say that a very important foundation which will administer only trust funds can invest as it sees fit. There must be some reason for it. I should certainly like to know exactly what the reason is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think
there is a misconception in the minds of the two hon. gentlemen who have just spoken. In Canada property and civil rights are within the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures. The only institutions with respect to which there is federal legislation as to investment are the banks, which are under the exclusive jurisdiction of parliament, the trust companies that are incorporated by federal statute, and the insurance companies that are registered under federal statute.
The provisions that exist for trusts that do not come within these three categories are provisions which exist under provincial legislation, and which are different in the several provinces. I do not know of any general law in the province of Quebec, with the exception of the civil code which deals with substitutions or with inheritances that have to pass through more than one series of beneficiaries, with respect to the investment of trust funds. I was for a time a member of the syndicat financier of Laval University, and I do not know that there was any legislative provision that required them to make their investments in any special form. I would not want to be too positive about that, but at the time I felt we were the ones who had to take the responsibility for determining the kind of investments that could be made out of the proceeds

of campaigns that had been quite successful in coming to the aid of that university.
I know that in several provinces there are statutory provisions of general application which deal with trust funds. There was no special reason in this case other than the feeling that the Canada Council is very apt to receive bequests of certain securities. I know of trust funds, for instance, that were set up for the Canadian Bar Association not out of cash turned over to the association but in specific securities turned over by the benefactors of the association.
Would the Prime Minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

Would the Prime Minister agree that in such cases any funds that are given can be given with a special provision that they are to be invested in a certain way? Does he think that affects the provisions governing this fund which is being put up by the public?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, I would not want to answer the hon. gentleman's question offhand without looking at the provisions in the bill with respect to gifts or bequests made to the Canada Council. I would imagine that even if provision was going to be made about the general investments of the Canada Council, this house would wish that to be expressed in such a way that it would not prevent the council from accepting a bequest that was made with the condition that it was to be invested in such and such a security.
I would have to read the sections of the bill to see whether or not that is already contained in the bill. Of course it was not required in view of the general terms of section 19, but if the general terms of section 19 were to be varied I would want to look at the other sections to see if there were other provisions that would require consequential amendment so as not to create obstacles to the acceptance of something that had a condition attached requiring it to be invested in such and such a way. I can assure hon. gentlemen that was the only reason, and that there was no thought or desire of putting this Canada Council in a position where it might lose any part of its endowment fund.
There never is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did feel that they might, probably under the terms of the Insurance Act, make some small portion of their investments in equities that were subject to enhancement in value because our country is growing and there are certain equity securities, or there probably could be

found certain equity securities, that would be apt to increase substantially in value. I do not think anyone would want to put very many eggs in the same basket. I think the persons responsible for the investments would want to have a pretty wide distribution of the investments with an eye both to a fair return and, for a certain portion of the proceeds, some capital increment.
It was felt that with this kind of an investment committee the investment would be apt to be spread out in that fashion. Of course economic conditions can be cyclical, but hon. gentlemen know that several of these investment organizations that have been set up in t'he last quarter of a century and have diversified their investments pretty broadly have shown a fair annual return and some of them a very substantial capital increment resulting from the broad nature of the securities in which they have made these investments. It was felt that with a properly constituted council and advisory board, they could be trusted to make wise investments.
This would not necessarily mean that they would appear wise a quarter of a century hence. There is always some uncertainty in these economic problems. However, there would not be much greater security in fixing as the limitation that which is imposed upon insurance companies, because we very frequently see on prospectuses that are not apt to be too impressive the statement that these securities qualify under the insurance act. The hon. gentleman must have noticed that line in advertisements in our newspapers concerning new issues of securities.
It may be there would be some feeling that they were going to have to take less responsibility if there were this same provision that exists in the insurance act. Again that is a matter upon which I would not feel qualified to express a firm opinion.

I appreciate very much the remarks that the Prime Minister has made. Certainly I would hope I have not given any indication that I object to any grant or endowment in stocks to the foundation. However, this is strictly on the question of investment. If my memory is correct almost all, and most certainly the majority, of the provinces have laid down regulations for the protection of trust funds, stating the manner in which investments may be made.
I know, so far as British Columbia is concerned, it is in first mortgage and government bonds; we are held down to that. By the way, if I may say this to the Prime Minister, that has not paid off very well, because the organization with which I am concerned has invested surplus funds in federal government bonds. Just recently we
Canada Council
needed some money but could not get it unless we took a loss of $8 per $100 on those government bonds.
If in the administration of trust funds it is set out by law that we have to stand a loss of 8 per cent on our capital investment in government bonds, in my opinion it is even more important as to how the funds of the council are going to be protected. I cannot understand why, if the majority of the provinces insist by legislation that investments in trust funds can only be done in a way which in the opinion of those who brought in the law is the best protection for the investment of those trust funds, the federal government gives wide open powers of investment under clause 19 of this bill. I believe if the provinces found legislation was required for the protection of trust funds, the federal government, in establishing a trust foundation, should give consideration to the same factors, especially in view of the fact that we lose money by investing in these government bonds.
May I ask at the same time, since this is a trust foundation administering a trust fund, and its headquarters are to be established in Ottawa, whether the investment of the trust fund will come under the legislation of Ontario?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it would be governed by the terms of this statute.

It appears to me that this is another clause that might be amended to some advantage. As the hon. member for Greenwood has pointed out, you are dealing in this case not with money contributed by individuals but with money contributed by the taxpayers of Canada. I cannot help but think there should be some restriction on how this money might be invested. With it wide open and with five men named, none of whom we know, except we have heard rumours as to one and have expectations as to another, with five members practically named for life, it is almost like putting them in the Senate.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: It is the same.

They may be fitted for the task and they may not. The 19 men administering this fund might be the greatest gamblers with the taxpayers' money we have ever had. They might buy real estate and make a lot of money; they might buy mining stock and double their money; they might buy oil wells and they might invest in dry wells. I can conceive of a lot of things they might invest in. They might invest in manufacturing industries.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Race horses.

Canada Council
Yes; they might even gamble on the chances of the Liberal party in the next election.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That is no gamble.
It is even more risky than a horse race.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: A sure bet.

There are all those wide open fields. I know none of us doubt the good intentions of the Prime Minister in this issue, and we do not doubt the good intentions of his government in establishing this council. After listening to what the Prime Minister had to say a few minutes ago I could not help but think one could not doubt his good intentions, but the longer he talked the wider became the field of possible errors.
I would hope that we could have an investment committee consisting of men of as wide experience in business and investment as the Prime Minister himself. In fact I think it would be well for him to give the five life appointees a little talk like the one he gave us today, and point out to them the dangers. There may be some who would be glad to have the appointment. There may be some on that council who were never very successful in their own investments. There may be some on the council who have already lost their own money and probably someone else's money, and may still be good characters. It is left wide open for them, you might say, without any disrespect to them, to gamble with someone else's money in whatever way they see fit.
Now, this is a lot of money. It is an important function for which this council is being established. It does appear to me that the Prime Minister, with the wide experience he has shown in this matter, should put some form of restriction on the investments. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said, it need not be investments with a trust company; but I feel it is unfair to the taxpayers of Canada to leave a wide open end, to name a committee for life and tell them to take the money and invest it as they like, in anything they see fit, in anything they think is going to be good.
As the Prime Minister said today, those of us who have tried to improve our own lot have made mistakes, at least some of us have. Perhaps some are too proud to admit it, but most people have made mistakes. I have heard of some who made mistakes and have regretted their investments. As the Prime Minister said, in 10 years' time the investments do not look the same; sometimes they do not look the same in five years. In fact

I have made some investments which did not. look the same in five days. They can switch pretty fast.
The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa said, "You may invest in a gamble on an even chance". That is ridiculous. I do not mean that. I am quite satisfied that the investment committee to be selected will consist of men who will, as the Prime Minister said, have good intentions; that is, the Prime Minister is hoping they will have good intentions. Well, as the Prime Minister knows, good intentions is the pathway of failure, or the pathway of failure is strewn with good intentions.
I do not know of anyone in this house- there may be some-who might not be in error in the next five years in investments in this country. It seems to me there should be some chart, something along the same line as a trust company's guide or an insurance company's guide. As has been mentioned, investments in government bonds are not always successful. The hon. member mentioned that he lost eight points on them. The Prime Minister quite neatly replied that probably he paid too much for them; maybe he did.
Seriously, it does appear to me that with a fund such as this you are not playing with your own money; you are playing with the public's money. It seems to me that you are a trustee or executor of it. If there are those of us who wish to gamble with our own money and, as they say on the street corner, take a flyer on something by investing a few thousand dollars or a few hundred dollars, as the case may be, that is all right. We take our chance. If we lose it we sometimes do not even tell our wives about it; but if we win we are lucky, and if we win a lot we probably hesitate to tell somebody who has been less fortunate for fear he may think we are bragging. But here we are dealing with trust funds. If any of us have been executors, as most of us have been, we will realize that. This committee more or less takes the form of an executor.
If I named two of my Liberal colleagues as my executor, Mr. Chairman, I would not expect them to start gambling with the little bit of money a farmer like myself might have. They might rob my whole family with good intentions; they might want to make my estate larger.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: They might do it on purpose.

No, I do not think they would do it on purpose. This is an executorship; therefore to my mind it should not be left wide open. This is not a matter of political differences; it is a matter of trying to set this council up soundly and in a non-partisan

way. In fairness and in all seriousness I urge the Prime Minister to give consideration to changing this clause so the investments would be in a certain type of security at a reasonable rate of interest with a minimum of risk of loss and a maximum of security for the fund.
The Canadian taxpayers do not expect this committee to double their money in some wildcat scheme or some investment, and they do not expect them, in an effort to enhance the fund, to risk it too much. It seems to me that the clause could be improved, and in all sincerity I urge the Prime Minister to give some thought to it.
We do not doubt the Prime Minister's good intentions nor do we doubt the good intentions of his appointees, but we are not infallible. For their benefit and for the security of the fund I would like to see reasonable safeguards fixed, as they are fixed for the insurance companies. The Prime Minister neatly said that he had noticed some of these balance sheets. It is true that sometimes we see what insurance companies are permitted to invest in. I think he is quite right when he says that to his mind some of them did not look to be too good, and probably they were not.
They at least must have a history.

That is true but, as he knows, some of the executors of trust companies have invested some of their own private family funds in investments they should not have made and have made some money in them, but there are times when it could be a very serious matter for an executor to take money and try to make ten to one on it and probably lose the whole thing.
We are not going to lose all this, but it appears to me that it would be safeguarded considerably if this suggestion was followed. I urge the Prime Minister to give some thought to applying some safeguards.

Mr. Chairman, I am somewhat encouraged, whether with or without grounds, to believe that the Prime Minister's mind is not closed on this subject; therefore I venture to add one or two points. In the first place we are morally, although not legally of course, the trustees of public money; therefore I should have thought that prima facie, we would deal as other trustees deal. We have the wisdom of generations or even centuries embodied in legislation. This is not primarily to guard against fraud but to guard against human frailty and human limitations.
When he was answering my question I rather expected the Prime Minister would

[Mr. Macdonnell.l

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would be very easy to find language that would accomplish what the hon. gentleman has in mind if it were felt that this would be a wise thing to do. The investments specified in the Insurance Act are merely, first of all, evidences of indebtedness, bonds or mortgages or something for a specific amount that was, let us say, $100 in 1925 and which is still $100 today with dollars that do not have the same real value they had in 1925; and in addition to the investments in securities or evidences of indebtedness stated in currency terms there is the possibility of investing as much as 15 per cent-
In common shares.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-in common shares on which dividends have been paid regularly for a period of seven years; and that means the things which are-to use the expression used a moment ago by the hon. member for Greenwood-the "blue chips" of the present era as far as common stocks are concerned.
These common stocks usually, if there are no other considerations affecting their value, in their increased prices on the market reflect the diminishing purchasing value of the currency. Shares that might have had, all other considerations being the same, a value of $100 in 1925 would probably have a value of $200 in the dollars of today. That is certainly a consideration. If it is felt it is better to tie this down to the number of currency units that exist today it would be easy to find the language to do it.
On the other hand, if it is felt that there can be such investments as would be more sensitive to the purchasing value of the unit of currency over a long period of time-this endowment that is being set up is for a very long period of time-we felt that it would be prudent to allow men of the calibre we expect to have for both the council and the investment committee to exercise their judgment based upon their own experience. When one says they are going to gamble with public

money he is just saying what might be legally possible but would not in fact be conceivable of those who would be entrusted with this responsibility.
We felt there was not apt to be very great advantage in restricting the investments to the kind set out in the insurance act.
Why is the investment of money standing to the credit of the university capital grants fund to be confined to bonds?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman was not here when I answered that question. The reason is that this is for only a short term, and government bonds are usually redeemable or convertible at any time. This amount may have to be realized in portions at times that cannot be fixed as maturities. It was for that reason that we thought we should have something that could be rapidly converted into cash; therefore this provision was inserted with respect to that part of the fund being placed at the disposal of the Canada Council.
As to the other point, the hon. gentleman and I have lived for a good many years and it is only in the last two or three decades that we have been impressed by the fact that currencies do change in value. For a long time currency in the popular mind was regarded as something quite stable.
The Minister of Finance is going to restore it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Ministers of finance have succeeded ministers of finance ever since 1867. For a period when there was no rapid development, no rapid change in the world, the pound sterling and other units of currency were regarded as the kind of things against which you could measure mutable things. They were immutable. The experience of the last quarter century or more has shown that that concept can no longer prevail, and that the best kind of investments are not always those that can be paid off in a specified number of units of currency. That has been the unfortunate experience of the last few decades.
To what extent an investment committee or a body like the Canada Council can guard a certain portion of its investment against situations of that kind only the future will really tell. I would not feel any safer about the future of this endowment if it were declared that it could be placed only in securities that are enumerated in the insurance act.

Mr. Chairman, I find myself in a rather devastated position because in the last few minutes I feel the Prime Minister has been making an argument in favour of the acceptance of continuous inflation. I do not know whether he read the article in the
Canada Council
Montreal Gazette of this morning, but I think it is one which everybody should read because it constitutes the argument of an authority who apparently thinks inflation is a nice thing, and therefore we should go along pleasantly with it. I think the Gazette gave a devastating answer.
The Prime Minister gave as an illustration a common stock which could have been bought for $100 in 1925 and which may be worth $200 today, but he forgot to point out that it might also be worth nothing at all today. Another thing I think the Prime Minister overlooked in connection with the amount of flexibility under the insurance act is that that act provides that in addition to common stocks being permissible, preferred stocks are also.
I do not think I need take more time of the committee. I am not convinced by the Prime Minister, and perhaps I had better move the amendment which I have prepared. I am glad there are at least some others in the committee who share my view that to give permission to invest in any manner the committee sees fit is just something that1 I do not think this committee should pass. Therefore I move as an amendment to section 19 (1) of the bill:
Delete the words "in any manner it see fit" in line 5 and insert after the word "otherwise" in line 8 the following:
"in such investments as are permitted for investment by insurance companies as set out in sections 63-66, both inclusive, of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1952, chapter 31, an act respecting Canadian and British insurance companies, or as amended from time to time."
The section would then read:
The council may, for the purposes of this act, acquire, hold, manage and dispose of real and personal property, and, subject to any other provision of this act relating thereto and on the advice of the investment committee, may invest any money standing to the credit of the endowment fund or the university capital grants fund or any money received by the council by gift, bequest or otherwise, in such investments as are permitted for investment by insurance companies as set out in sections 63-66 (both inclusive) of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1952, chapter 31, an act respecting Canadian and British insurance companies or as amended from time to time, and may hold, manage and dispose of any such investment.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, what I am moving is that the powers be restricted to the powers under the insurance act which, I argue, give them all the latitude which should properly be given.

Mr. Chairman, I have been very much interested in the attitude of the Prime Minister toward these investments, and if I understood him correctly he said that the prices of common stocks more or less reflect the true value of the dollar. I am afraid I do not agree.

Mr. Chairman, there is one further point which arises on this clause. It seems to me there is a possibility of contradiction in two phrases of the clause which might eventually lead to misunderstanding. As the Prime Minister has been so good about neutralizing himself in the previous debate, perhaps he may agree with this as well. Section 19 (1) uses these words:
The council-on the advice of the investment committee, may invest in any manner it sees fit any money standing to the credit of the endowment fund or the university capital grants fund-
Now it would be possible and, I think, quite logical to read "on the advice of" as the equivalent of "subject to the advice of", and if we accept that interpretation we have a contradiction. While we read that the council shall act "subject to the advice of the investment committee", we also state they may invest in any manner that they see fit. This last is definite because we have this afternoon decided that they may invest in any manner they see fit.
I am wondering whether it would not be advisable to make it quite clear in this section that the investment committee is purely an advisory body, and is not one which has any power of control over the investments of the council. That is made clear under section 18, subsection 2, where it says:

The investment committee shall aid and advise the council in making, managing and disposing of investments under this act.
But when we reach the next section, we find this position, and I think the best illustration I can use to show the force of the words is one which will be familiar to every hon. member of this house. The Governor General acts on the advice of his ministers, and certainly that terminology is taken to mean, and has meant for a long time, that he acts subject to the advice of his ministers.
If we turn to the definition in the dictionary-I have just one here, and it is the Concise Oxford-we find the word "on" defined as meaning "supported by". There are further phrases given-"attached to", "covering" and so on-which are not pertinent. But essentially it does mean in that context "subject to", and I would recommend, if it is agreeable to the Prime Minister -I am not going to move an amendment at this point-that we should consider the advisability of dropping the phrase "on the advice of the investment committee" and replacing it by some phrase such as "subject to the provisions of section 18, subsection 2", which would make the position quite clear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, it was intended to make this advisory committee a useful body and not just an ornament that could be consulted or not as the council chose. The council is not obliged to make an investment recommended by the committee, but it would not have the right to make investments other than among those recommended by the committee. It is not to have a free choice to go ahead and make any kind of investment it sees fit to make unless it is an investment that is within the advice given to it by the investment committee, and that is the intention.

That clarifies the position in the mind of the Prime Minister, but it leaves me still with the feeling that there is this contradiction. The Prime Minister has said that if the council makes an investment the investment must first have been recommended to it by the investment committee. It might recommend a slate of investments from which the council could choose. Under this circumstance we have the reverse contradiction, because we have the council investing "in any manner it sees fit."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

Subject to the provisions of the act. For example, one of the provisions of the act is that with respect to the capital grants fund, moneys can be invested only in government of

Will the Prime Minister not agree with me that when the clause says, "may invest in any manner it sees fit"-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If there is nothing else that is what it means, but with these qualifications that are in the clause it does not have the broad meaning it would otherwise have.

Does the Prime Minister not see any possibility of an eventual conflict in reasoning in this clause, in which we have the Canada Council specifically given authority to invest in any manner it sees fit, but on the advice of the investment committee? It seems to me that the one phrase gives the council all-embracing power and the second qualifies it, without specifically striking a balance. I am wondering whether we could not find a slight change in that phrase so there would be no misunderstanding in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND BENEFITS AND PROVIDE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it will be remembered that municipal grants were first paid on federal property from January 1, 1950, under the municipal grants regulations,

Municipal Grants Act
and that these were made statutory the following year. In their original form the annual grants were paid to the extent of 75 per cent of the tax applicable on the value of federal property in excess of 4 per cent of the aggregate of taxable and federal property in the municipality. The figure used was derived from a survey of property ownership in municipalities in 1947.
This original formula was applied in the determination of grants in lieu of taxes for five years and, while of interest to but a limited number of municipalities, undoubtedly was of considerable assistance where there was a concentration of federal property. By the end of 1954, 48 municipalities were in receipt of annual grants totalling about $3 million.
Hon. members will recall that amendments were made to the Municipal Grants Act in 1955, broadening substantially the scope of the grants. In the light of experience gained in five years of operation it was decided to extend the legislation by reducing the minimum percentage or floor from 4 per cent to 2 per cent and to provide that municipalities would receive full payments on eligible property in excess of this minimum. These amendments resulted in larger annual payments to municipalities already qualifying for grants and in an increase in the number of municipalities eligible to receive them. Municipalities receiving grants under the general formula, known as section 5 grants, increased in number from 48 to the present 150. Total payments in the current fiscal year are estimated at $9J million.
As I have indicated on previous occasions, the government has kept under constant study the whole problem of the taxation of crown properties. There is no doubt in my mind that while the original grant formula was sound in principle, conditions have been constantly changing and have justified a more comprehensive approach. Much of the argument advanced for the extension of the program has been on the ground of municipal fiscal need, but this is a provincial matter and not the purpose of a bill of this nature. What we are concerned with here is the effect of the location of federal property within a municipality upon its capacity to perform its proper functions.
It is most difficult to draw any precise line to distinguish those properties which are performing a purely local function from those that have a wider use. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether I might have unanimous consent to complete the statement so hon. members will have it on the record, rather than call it five o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND BENEFITS AND PROVIDE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: If it is a brief statement I will not see the clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND BENEFITS AND PROVIDE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Rather than restrict the application of these grants, the government now proposes to remove the 2 per cent floor and pay grants to all municipalities with federal property where the normal municipal services in that municipality are performed on account of the federal property. This means that the federal government will, subject to certain exceptions, pay the equivalent of full municipal taxes, including school taxes, on its land and buildings in municipal areas.
Question has been raised in the past as to why these special exceptions are necessary. I think anyone who has seriously considered this matter will accept the fact that the government is not an ordinary taxpayer. The exemption of government property from taxation has existed since time immemorial. It is a principle generally accepted throughout the world and nowhere receives greater adherence than in the provinces themselves, of whom the municipalities are legal creatures. The special position that government functions occupy in the community is in itself the justification of this approach. In point of fact, many of the exceptions made are of a class commonly exempted in municipal taxing policy, as in the case of parks, museums, etc. Most of the exceptions stand as they are now contained in the present act. The principal change relates to large, self-contained defence establishments.
Formerly these were excluded from the grants base by the fact that they received no material services from municipalities; but as this criterion of material services has been removed, some special provision was necessary. These properties provide virtually all their own services and are largely independent of the municipality. However, recognition has been taken of the fact that the land they occupy is taken out of taxation, so provision is being made for a grant in lieu of taxes upon that land as well as upon federally-owned domestic establishments occupied by servants of the crown.
It has been found necessary to provide for one further special case where there are special circumstances following from heavy concentration of federal property in one municipality. This is a saving clause. Under this provision adjustments in the grants may be provided where the normal application of the act might not be appropriate in view of the relationship of other federal agencies to the affairs of the municipality. The best example of this sort of thing that comes to my mind is the position of the town of Oromocto in New Brunswick at the present time. This is a planned project connected

with Camp Gagetown, where special arrangements have been entered into with the province of New Brunswick for its management and development.
These are the most important changes proposed, but certain other provisions might also bear mention at this time. One will permit the payment of grants to local taxing authorities which are not strictly municipalities in the commonly accepted sense. This would cover local improvement districts and other quasi-municipal bodies having the power to levy real estate taxes in their own right. A further provision will allow payments on buildings owned and occupied by the crown where located on land leased from tax-exempt owners. These are now excluded by a technicality of the definition of federal property. A provision has been made for the adjustment of the applicable tax rates where municipalities have not taken into account the grants in setting the rates. This has been carried over from section 8, grants for domestic establishments which are now absorbed into the general grant structure. Of the remaining kinds of grants authorized in the present act, those in lieu of local improvement taxes will be continued, as will the transitional grants if the property concerned does not qualify for the annual grants.
The rural grants authorized by regulation under section 10, along with the section 8 grants for crown-owned domestic establishments, will be merged into the new general provisions under section 5. Authority will be continued under section 10 to pass regulations for supplementary payments to municipalities that do not contain federal property but that formerly shared in the area distribution of rural grants.

As I said earlier, these amendments will result in payments going to virtually every municipality in Canada that contains federal property which receives the normal municipal services of that municipality.
