subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext:
The second reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, involves endorsing the principle of the bill. I find this very difficult to do. I have been sent here by the people of my riding as a legislator, not to sit in judgment on other fellow citizens of mine. I feel that when I endorse the principle of this bill I am deserting the field of being a legislator and moving over into a field of which I know nothing.
In a former year the Prime Minister stated that this parliament is not really a divorce court at all, but that it has to grant to each and every individual citizen his primary right-whatever word he used for that

to bring his petition to the foot of the throne for relief, and parliament merely decided whether or not to grant such a petition. If that is to be taken to be what we are actually doing, then I should like to submit, as I have submitted before, that the same right must be granted to every citizen in Canada. This parliament cannot distinguish between citizens living in one or two provinces of Canada and citizens living in other provinces; after all, there may be citizens in other provinces who are not satisfied with divorce arrangements within their provinces, and they may also wish to bring petition to the foot of the throne.
On this subject of the endorsation of divorce, I happen to belong to a church that does not even believe in annulments, not to mention divorce. A few minutes ago a colleague of mine asked, "do you believe in divorce?" I honestly think I answered correctly when I said, "I have not yet made up my mind". This is basically a moral and religious problem. I rather feel that this
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]
parliament is exceeding its authority when it begins to settle moral and religious problems of its citizens. If it is the legal aspect we are thinking of, then certainly we are far removed from dispensing justice in this matter.
I understand that some new rules for the divorce committee of the other place are now being adopted, or were adopted yesterday. They may help some, and may prevent some of the flagrant violations of elementary court rules.
We in this C.C.F. group have been waiting now for many years for the government to come forth with a proposal that would be acceptable to at least most of the hon. members so we could be relieved of this obligation. In fact many of these divorce bills have for many years received the endorsation of this house because of the good will that obtained in all sections of the house. I believe it is technically within the power, or would have been within the power, of almost any one of us to block the whole machinery, had we not been men of good will heretofore.
The second reading, or the endorsation of the principle of a divorce bill, is I believe, usually meant to be based on the evidence submitted before a committee of the other place. I should rather say before one of the subcommittees of the divorce committee of the other place. Certainly the load is getting so heavy now that they actually have a number of subcommittees, and this particular case was heard by subcommittee No. 3.
I agree that these bills are all referred to the miscellaneous private bills committee of this house after they receive second reading and I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how right we are in following that procedure. I think I am safe in saying that very few members in this chamber have received, not to speak of reading, the evidence that was given before the committee of the other place.
A year ago I noted that we had to fill in a form or write a letter to the clerk of the other place and inform him whether we wished to be placed on the mailing list to receive this information. However, this afternoon I spoke to one member of our own miscellaneous private bills committee, and he had not received any of the minutes of proceedings and evidence taken at the hearing in the other place. How members of parliament can be expected to endorse the principle of a bill the name of which they see only on the order paper and of which they know nothing else is beyond me. However, we are expected to do so.
I am not at all satisfied to endorse the principle of a divorce bill on the basis of

the evidence I receive in my mail. I notice that in this particular case the evidence was heard by one man in his 79th year, another one in his 77th year and a new recruit who is in his 46th year. We, of course, are expected to be good boys, to be good sports about this whole matter; and in the ordinary course of events I assume we likely would have passed the 107 divorce bills on the order paper today in a matter of a couple of minutes.
As I said before, we have given the government every possible chance to find a remedy. They have never at any time indicated to us in this house that they are earnestly searching for that remedy. A few years ago the newspapers said the government was searching for some new method, but we have never had that report confirmed in this house.
I wish to make it perfectly clear here that what I am saying has nothing whatsoever in particular to do with the personal affairs of Dorothy Amelia Ashmore MacDonald, any more than with any of the other cases. However, when we wait year after year and the problem continues to grow; when we hold back a bill which we have presented a number of times and which would limit rather than broaden the grounds for divorce, but would transfer it to a proper court; when it is turned down when it is presented and we sit back and await action by the government-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext:
Order. I assure the hon. member that I am not interrupting because I want to. I have been sitting here trying to do two things at once, namely trying to enable the hon. member to discuss as fully as he might wish the matter before us, and at the same time trying not to allow him to go too far beyond what I believe the rules would permit at the present time.
I am going to take a minute of the time of the house, now that I feel impelled to rise to my feet, to quote a statement made by Mr. Speaker in 1955 when the situation was similar to what it is now. We were commencing the first discussion of divorce bills of the session and at that time Mr. Speaker said, as reported at page 116 of the 1955 Journals:
May I interrupt the hon. member to remind him that we are at the beginning of a new session. During previous sessions we have had debates as to how these divorce bills shall be dealt with on second reading. It being the beginning of a new session perhaps one may be permitted to adopt a new resolution. I have resolved that no matter how much latitude I may be inclined to give I shall not allow any discussion except that which relates to the principle of the bill. I do not think hon. members will find that they are referring to the principles of these bills when they stand up and
Private Bill-Divorce
offer suggestions as to how they should be dealt with. That is not the manner in which this can be brought about.
If the hon. member wishes to submit by way of a bill some other method by which these divorce bills can be dealt with, he will have ample opportunity to incorporate whatever suggestions he may have to offer. But I do not think it is in order on the second reading of these bills to make such suggestions, and I would like the hon. member's co-operation in respect to this point.
That is the end of the quotation from Mr. Speaker's ruling in 1955, to which I perhaps might take the liberty of adding an observation of my own. The principle of this bill, I think, has been read into the record by the hon. member who has the floor. It is the principle that if certain circumstances are proven it is expedient that a divorce should be given to this couple. I would not rule out of order any discussion at this time on the merits or demerits of the principle of divorce, because I think the principle of divorce is certainly applicable to the principle of a divorce bill; but I would ask the hon. member and others who may follow him to try with me to appreciate the difference between the principle of divorce and the principle of the forum in which divorce actions should be heard.
I think that principle was amply demonstrated some years ago when we had on the order paper several divorce bills similar to the one we are now discussing. We also had on the order paper and under discussion a bill which, had it passed, would have transferred the hearing of divorce bills from this chamber to another forum. There was nothing conflicting in those two bills because they had two separate and entirely different principles. I think the hon. member who has the floor and others will realize the difference between those principles, and will try to stay with the principles that are involved in this bill and not deal with those principles involved in a bill which we discussed some years ago and which did not pass, relative to the location of the court or forum where divorces should be heard.

subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. If we do not agree with the principle that this divorce be granted I note that you read what Mr. Speaker told the house on a former occasion, when he suggested that an amendment could be moved; and at the conclusion of my remarks, which I have just about completed, I intend to move such an amendment.
I said on a former occasion that if necessary the day may come when I may have to deal with all the horrible details of these divorce cases. I do not intend to begin doing so today, but I repeat the warning that the

Private Bill-Divorce
day may arrive when we may become involved in a discussion as to whether the panties in a specific case were pink or blue in colour.
However, this is a serious matter. In the particular case before us a girl seven years of age is involved. We are endorsing the principle that this couple be granted a divorce, but at the same time we are shrugging off any responsibility for the child seven years old. We say that has to be settled by some other court or forum. In this case we have witnesses who leave much to be desired.
However, I am not going to discuss the details of this case at greater length at this moment. Instead I shall resort to what I think is the only weapon available to us- if I may use the word weapon-which I think we can properly apply and remain gentlemen and legislators. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That Bill No. 17 be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.
I think we should know something about these bills before we endorse the principle of them. Most of us have not even read the bills.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a brief word in support of the amendment, the purpose of which is to ask that this particular case be studied by the committee on miscellaneous private bills before the house approves second reading rather than after this is done.
As my colleague the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has already indicated, there is a child involved in this case, and we feel that some questions might be asked in addition to the questions that were asked in the other place with reference to the financial support the father has provided or has failed to provide for his child.
The other comment I wish to make is that this case does seem to entail some rather strange bits of evidence. In one instance where certain evidence was offered and an attempt was made to confirm that evidence the witness admitted having written to the hotel in question, only to be informed by letter that the hotel did not keep records for more than three years. The incident introduced as evidence of misconduct had taken place five years earlier; hence the strength of the evidence on that point seems to be rather slight.
Another point in the evidence that is rather interesting concerned an incident where a witness was called who admitted
[Mr. Regier.l
that he was the proprietor of a tourist home, and the evidence put in related to something that happened in the tourist home located next door to his establishment. The witness who was called admitted that he was not there but that he was looking after the next-door tourist home more or less by remote control.
These pieces of evidence do not strike us as very satisfactory, and we think it is a reasonable and responsible suggestion we are making in this amendment, namely that before we are asked to approve the principle of this bill by giving it second reading we should send its subject matter to a committee of this house for study by that committee. I therefore support the amendment which has been moved by my colleague the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.

subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although this bill stands in my name I do not wish to express any opinion concerning it, as did the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I might say that the hon. gentleman has voiced the very reason we should deal with this bill. He commenced to read into the record the words contained in the bill, and Mr. Speaker prevented him from continuing.
We in this chamber have a serious responsibility with regard to the granting of divorce, as have those members of the other place and all those who serve on divorce committees. Under the rules and regulations and legislation governing divorce there are four different bodies involved, whereas in other parts of the country a divorce or annulment is granted by a single court.
I take objection to what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said, to the effect that he was incompetent to pass judgment upon his fellow citizens. As far as matters before the committee are concerned I feel I must disagree with him. I had the privilege of being chairman of the committee during last session, and I found the hon. member to be a most competent judge of the matters brought before the committee. He fulfilled his duties carefully, with a great deal of detailed attention and understanding.
The hon. member has brought up another matter, and has contended that there should not be different methods of obtaining divorce in different parts of Canada, that all citizens should be treated alike. By the legislation and the rules and regulations governing divorce we make it possible for all the people of Canada to have available this procedure for divorce. If there is no divorce court or provision for the granting of divorce in the province in which the petitioner resides or

has his domicile, he is given the same opportunity as someone else who lives across the border in another province to obtain a divorce by coming to this body. He is placed on an equal basis with other Canadians.
We should take cognizance of the fact that we have a responsibility toward the citizens of Canada, and whether we term this a matter of legislation or passing judgment on our fellow citizens, we should do our best to arrive at a determination of these matters. It is our responsibility to handle these divorce matters in a proper manner.
Having had some experience on committees I cannot see the point in the amendment moved by the hon. member. He has indicated that he is doing this to bring about new divorce legislation, but if that were done we would possibly be depriving the two people mentioned in the petition of their right as citizens of Canada to have their marriage dissolved.
I have always felt that when these bills got to the committee stage the evidence as received from the Senate committee was fairly well reviewed. I do not think aspersions should be cast upon the members of the Senate committee, one being 79 years of age and another being 46 years of age. If we consider the history of the courts of this country or of any other country we will find that many gentlemen have sat upon the bench who had passed the age of 79 years and still were able to deliver sound judgments. Probably the older we get the greater stock of experience we have behind us to help us pass judgment on facts with which we have to deal. I am sure the gentlemen who sit on the committee in the other place would grace the bench of any court in this land or for that matter any other land.
Our procedure is to refer these bills to the committee on miscellaneous private bills after they have received second reading. When the bills reach that committee they are reviewed by intelligent members of the committee. Some members of the committee have made inquiries personally in order to assist the committee in deciding certain matters. I cannot see the point at' this stage of referring the subject matter of a bill of this nature to the committee before it has received second reading.
Since this matter has been brought up I am sure my hon. friends have noticed that there have been amendments to the regulations concerning divorce. Before dealing with that I may say that these petitions for legislation are before us and it is our duty to consider them and do our job as legislators. I understand that the Senate has made a change in the rules governing divorce. This change was enacted yesterday,
Private Bill-Divorce
St. Valentine's day, and provides that after September 1, 1957, a petition for divorce, according to my interpretation of the change in the rule, must contain the name of the corespondent or third party to the petition. Hitherto this party was not named in the petition.
However, that being the case, the defendant and the corespondent now will have the right to defend the petition, and no harm will be done to an innocent party as some hon. members of this house may feel could have happened before. As we know, we are now adopting a change by which we would be bringing the rules of the divorce committee in line with those of some of the provinces that have divorce courts. And I might say it seems there is another change in the rules respecting divorce, as I understand it, to the effect that if the name of the corespondent cannot be determined, as I understand was the case in 356 cases last year, as in the provincial divorce courts, now they have a provision that an action cannot be brought in such circumstances unless the party bringing the action is able to do so by leave of the court.
If we were to take, for example, the laws of the province of Ontario, and if we would refer to our rules of practice in Ontario, we would find that rule 776 reads as follows:
If the name of any person with whom an adultery is alleged to have been committed is unknown to the plaintiff at the time of the issue of the writ, the judge, on being satisfied that all reasonable efforts have been made to ascertain the name may grant leave to the plaintiff to issue a writ without adding such person as a defendant.
Now if we apply the rule as reported in the other place I think a great many of the difficulties which probably are presently worrying my hon. friends may be removed; and once again, as I say, all citizens of Canada will be put on an even basis as far as obtaining divorce is concerned. At least if we would apply the rule of the province of Ontario they would all be the same in that respect.
There is, of course, another advantage. I know some of my hon. friends have been worried about the question of investigators. Possibly many of us have taken a second look at that problem, so they are not alone in that. But when it comes to the point where the third, or outside, party must be named, it seems to me there will be a great deal more discretion used than in the past. I understand, if I have the right interpretation of the application of the new rules in the other place, that when there are situations where the outside party, or corespondent as we might prefer to call him in the civil courts, cannot be found or named or identified, there would be provision for this eventuality. If

Private Bill-Divorce
not, there should be a provision made whereby with the leave of those in charge of petitions the matter would be allowed to go forward without the name of the corespondent.
I know the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam wishes to change the rules in the amendment he proposes. I think it would be unwise to ask to change the rules governing divorce at a time when the other house has taken up this matter. I think we, as legislators here and as people and citizens of Canada, should first look at the pros and cons of this matter to see whether we approve or disapprove of the bill before us, and in no way prejudice those who are applying themselves to this one particular divorce petition, the petition of Dorothy Amelia Ashmore MacDonald. We should in no way prejudice these people, or any of the others who have put forward petitions in accordance with the rules and regulations now in existence. Mrs. MacDonald has asked these two houses of parliament for relief in the circumstances in which she presently finds herself.
That being the case, and going back again to the question of responsibility which one of my hon. friends has mentioned and which we have as legislators, we should accept our responsibility now and pass this under the rules and regulations and under the legislation which we presently have, leaving it to the committee to decide upon the evidence and awaiting their recommendation to this house.
We always have our opportunity in this chamber, on the third reading of these bills, to raise any objections we might have to clauses in the bills, the preamble, the title of the bill and the passing of the bill, and it seems premature at this point to do anything which might delay the proper procedure which we have before us. As I have stated, we have an amendment to the regulations of the other house concerning divorce. We now find ourselves under this method we have adopted in the position of not giving the amended rules an opportunity of dealing with divorce petitions.

subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext: Hang on for ten minutes and you will have talked it out.

subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext:
As I have said, although the bill happens to be in my name I have no personal opinions to express. Nevertheless, if the bill is given second reading and referred to the committee, with which I have something to do, I am quite sure it will be thoroughly considered by the members of that committee. I conclude by saying that I think there should be an opportunity for members to express themselves at this time.

The hon. member for Vancouver East said a moment ago that I should keep talking to talk out the bill, but I leave it now with the remarks I have made.

subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have noticed the obvious distaste with which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has spoken about this bill, and I rather think the only reason he spoke on it at all was that he was not very anxious to have the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company bill discussed during this hour.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext: Order. I do not think I should allow that statement to stand.

subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext: I will be glad to withdraw it, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps my weak attempt at humour did not strike a responsive chord in all quarters of the house. To be quite serious, I believe the divorce procedure is certainly not in accord with the wishes of the great majority of members of the house, and it is a matter to which I have given a great deal of thought since I have been here. I believe there have been some minor improvements in the procedure. I for one think there was a very definite improvement in the procedure in the last year or so, when instead of all 266 members of the House of Commons getting all the evidence in all of the cases-does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre wish to say something?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext: I was wondering where the hon. member got the extra member. There are only 265.

subtopic: DOROTHY AMELIA ASHMORE MACDONALD
speechtext:
Well, I will not quarrel with the hon. member. I think there was a definite improvement when we ceased having to wade through the long and rather odious records of the proceedings.
Speaking for a moment on the concrete proposal of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I think it might be rather unfair to single out this particular person in this particular way with all the publicity that has been given to the matter, and especially by way of redressing some kind of grievance involving a seven year old child. It seems to me the only result would be to create additional hardship for a youngster who has had enough hardship already.
We all know that the vast majority of these divorce bills that come before the house come from one or two parts of the country. One thing that troubles the conscience of all members of parliament who have to take even a very minor part in the passing of these divorce bills is the knowledge, as has been pointed out a good many

times in the past few years, that in a good many cases there has not been adequate attention given to the family injustice that is a by-product of this form of separation. I for one have often wondered whether it would not be at least an improvement in the method of procedure if we made it a prior condition of the legislative form of divorce that all applications from the province of Quebec, the province of Newfoundland or any province should be preceded by legal separations in the province where the applications originate. In other words, the family affairs should be dealt with by the proper and competent bodies before applications for divorce are made to the agency of the parliament of Canada charged with dealing with them.
I for one am an advocate of a changed system of divorce, but I must confess that on examining the actual procedures in this exalted building I have had to revise some of the preconceptions I had before I came to this place. I think the actual procedures in the examination of divorce evidence followed by the committees of the other place will compare very favourably with the procedures of any court in the whole Dominion of Canada or, for that matter, any court in the civilized world. There is great dignity and complete fairness to all parties. There are no facilities for sensationalism in any way, shape or form. There is fair play
Private Bill-Divorce
to all concerned in the case and the whole matter is carried on in as dignified, fair and judicial a manner as possible in any kind of constituted court.
Therefore it seems to me that no matter what anyone may suggest as to changing the procedure for the handling of divorces, one thing that cannot be achieved by any change in the technique of divorce is the getting of any more fair or judicial method of handling them.
On motion of Mr. Philpott the debate was adjourned.

PINKERTON DETECTIVE AGENCY
speechtext:
What was the amount paid to the Pinkerton detective agency by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, during the calendar year of 1956?
Answer by: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
The corporation advises that during 1956 the Pinkerton detective agency provided night protection service to its television station in Ottawa. In addition, the services of this agency were used on special occasions for the
protection of television equipment used on outside broadcasts.
It has been held that it would be disadvantageous to the corporation in business negotiations to make public amounts of payments to individual persons or organizations for services provided.
